entry.title: ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS BUY CLEVELAND FIVE INNINGS AND NOT AN OUT MORE — VOGT LIFTS WILLIAMS AT HIS EIGHT-AND-NINETIETH PITCH, THE SIXTH COMES APART IN RELIEF, AND MONTGOMERY'S TWO-RUN DOUBLE SENDS CHICAGO HOME NEEDING ONE: WHITE SOX 4, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 90 · Tuesday, the Sixth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS BUY CLEVELAND FIVE INNINGS AND NOT AN OUT MORE — VOGT LIFTS WILLIAMS AT HIS EIGHT-AND-NINETIETH PITCH, THE SIXTH COMES APART IN RELIEF, AND MONTGOMERY'S TWO-RUN DOUBLE SENDS CHICAGO HOME NEEDING ONE: WHITE SOX 4, GUARDIANS 3

The hardest arm on the lakefront fans eleven with 18 pitches at 100 miles the hour or better, hands a one-run lead to his bullpen after a leadoff single in the sixth, and watches it burn — Sabrowski walking the pinch-hitter Grichuk on four pitches, uncorking a wild pitch, and standing one short fly from escape when Braden Montgomery lines a two-run double the opposite way; Sean Burke retires 13 in a row in bulk relief, Grant Taylor survives Adell's first-pitch triple to close the 4-3 verdict, and the Pale Hose — who trailed for the first time all postseason after an unearned two-run first — fly home with four October victories, all of them taken on the road, one win from a first Championship Series since 2005 and a first home playoff clincher since the World Series of 1906

For five innings and one batter Monday evening, the argument belonged to the heaviest artillery this paper promised. Gavin Williams was everything Cleveland's predicament required: eleven strikeouts, five of them in unbroken succession from the end of the first inning to the top of the third — no Cleveland pitcher had ever done that in October — and 18 pitches at 100 miles the hour or better, tying Emmanuel Clase's franchise mark of the whole tracking era. He became but the third Cleveland man to reach double figures in strikeouts in a postseason game, one shy of Charles Nagy's record twelve of 1996, and he carried a 2-1 lead into the sixth.5 The lead itself had been staked in the first, and not honestly earned: Kwan's leadoff single off the opener Kay, a pass to Ramírez, an intentional walk around Adell — and then Lowe's comebacker to the second relayman Newcomb, whose throw sailed past Murakami at first while two runs crossed. Thus did the White Sox trail in a 2026 postseason game for the first time, their streak expiring at 27 innings, 24 of them led, as this paper's columns had counted them.3

Then came the hinge on which Cleveland's whole October may yet swing. Miguel Vargas — the one Chicago batsman giving Williams honest trouble, with two walks already to his evening — led off the sixth with a single to left, and the manager Vogt, his starter at 98 pitches, went to the bullpen. "If he has to face two more hitters, now you're running him up to 110, 115," Vogt reasoned afterward. "It was the right time to get him out of there. He pitched his backside off. Just unfortunate we were not able to get the result." The left-hander Sabrowski, nearly untouchable since August, chose this night to have nothing: Murakami's groundout moved the runner, Grichuk walked on four pitches, a wild pitch advanced the pair, and after Pham's short fly to left brought escape within a single out, Braden Montgomery — a rookie who has labored all season from the right side — lined a two-run double down the right-field line. Gaddis relieved and was greeted by Meidroth's run-scoring single, and a 2-1 Cleveland lead had become a 4-2 Chicago one, five batters wide. "Just lack of control," said Sabrowski. "It's unfortunate. It was a pretty big part of the game, and I let a lot of guys down."5

The relay that followed was the one this paper sketched in Monday's columns, run precisely to the drawing. Sean Burke, the staff's ace recast as a man of bulk, gave five innings and a third on one hit and one run, striking out six and at one stretch retiring 13 in succession — tied for the second-longest such run by a reliever in any postseason game, behind only Bumgarner's 14 in the seventh game of the 2014 World Series.4 "Tip your cap to Burke, what an unbelievable performance," ruled Vogt. "He was mixing and matching, criss-crossing away, criss-crossing in." Kwan testified that the fastball "just had a little extra life on it." Murakami's fourth-inning single had meanwhile cashed Teel for Chicago's first run, and when Burke yielded a two-out single to DeLauter in the eighth, the closer Taylor — twelve outs of save on Saturday, seven pitches wanted Monday — was greeted rudely: Adell's first-pitch triple to the left-center gap, a foot or two of wall shy of a tying home run, scored DeLauter to make it 4-3. Lowe then lined to left, where Antonacci ran the ball down at full stretch, and Taylor's ninth went three up, three down for the save.3

So Chicago, which has not played a home game this October, carries two victories to Rate Field, where Wednesday's third game goes at 4 o'clock Eastern before a sellout that will wear the Blackout in broad daylight. The arithmetic is stern for the hosts-to-be-visitors: clubs ahead two games to none in a best-of-five have gone through 83 times in 93, and clubs that took the first two on the road under the present format 17 times in 19; the last side to climb from such a hole was the 2017 Yankees — at Cleveland's own expense, the Guardians will not need reminding, though they may prefer the omen that they played better on the road (44-37) than at home this summer.36 Cleveland had named no starter by press time — Bibee, Griffin, and Cantillo, whose September behind the opener Espino ran 15 scoreless innings with 17 strikeouts, are the candidates, and Williams himself volunteers for the bullpen on one day's rest — while Chicago's likeliest man is the rookie Smith, author of 5 2/3 scoreless innings this postseason.6 The stakes on the South Side want no embroidery: one victory sends the White Sox to a first Championship Series since the 11-and-1 champions of 2005, and would seal the club's first home playoff clincher since the 14th of October, 1906, when they beat the Cubs at South Side Park for the title — 120 years gone. "It's going to be unbelievable. Those fans deserve it," said Taylor. "They have been with us for three years of 100 losses." Cleveland's answer came from Kwan, and it was steady as ever: "There's no panic button. We're not trying to do too much."3

The Postseason Card

THE GLOVES OF GOTHAM GIVE FOUR TIMES AND THE FIFTH INNING COLLECTS IN FULL — RICE'S PAIR OF CIRCUIT CLOUTS STANDS ALONE AGAINST A RALLY OF SINGLES AND SHOE LEATHER: GULF COAST CLUB 5, PINSTRIPES 2

The league's most un-strikeout-able order plays its signature hand — Aranda's single and Caminero's 112.4-mile double opening a four-run fifth finished by Simpson's legs, a stolen base, another New York misplay, and Palacios' two-run single on the eighth pitch of his turn — while Schlittler, the presumptive Cy Young choice of the scribes, is wrung for the fewest strikeouts of his career, two; Ben Rice homers twice on changeups and becomes the first Yankee ever to post two multi-homer games in a single postseason, Jones' fly ball strikes the B-ring catwalk and is patiently caught, and the top seed flies north two games to none — Game 3 Wednesday at eight in the Bronx, Fried against Martinez, with New York's season on the board

The Rays were asked before the game for their plan against Cam Schlittler, the young road warrior whose new curveball this paper admired only yesterday, and the shortstop Walls gave the answer of a man with nothing to hide: "Just kind of do what we've been doing all year." What they have done all year is strike out less than any club in the majors and put the ball upon the ground until something gives, and Monday night at Tropicana Field, before a sold-out house of 40,226, what gave was the New York infield. The first inning yielded a run without an earned deed in it — McMahon fumbling Díaz's grounder, Aranda singling, and Chisholm throwing away the force at second as Díaz crossed — one of three New York errors in that frame alone and four on the night, charged to four different gloves. Schlittler, for only the third time in his young career, finished his first two innings without a strikeout.7

Ben Rice answered alone. In the fourth he turned on a Peralta changeup — a pitch that had yielded no extra-base hit since the right-hander crossed to Tampa Bay — and found the right-field seats to square the account; in the eighth he did it again, off a Seymour changeup, and the scribes' ledger opened wide. Rice is the first man in the franchise's 61 postseason appearances to post two multi-homer games in a single October, and the first player in all postseason history to do it within his club's first four games; his five home runs in his first ten postseason games trail only Bernie Williams' six among Yankees, and his four this October tie Gehrig's 1928 for the second-most in the club's first four games of an autumn, behind Stanton's five of 2020. He is also, the instruments attest, the first man since the tracking began to hit two changeups out in a single postseason game.8 Between his salvos the game was settled: Booser wriggled New York's bases-loaded fifth shut, and in the home half Aranda singled, Caminero doubled at 112.4 miles the hour, Hicks grounded a run home, Simpson beat a ball that the shortstop Lombard could not corral, stole second, and watched DeLuca reach on Lombard's error before Palacios — second on the club this season with 31 two-out runs batted in — lined a two-run single up the middle on the eighth pitch of the turn. Four runs, one inning, scarcely a ball struck hard but one. "Constant pressure, constant long at-bats," said the manager Cash. "It's our M.O. all season long."7

The evening's curiosity arrived in the second, when Jones' towering fly struck the B-ring catwalk beneath the dome's roof and hung an age before Mesa settled under it for the out — a lawful catch under the house rules, the higher two rings being in play, and the second piece of October architecture to side with the home nine in three days, the roof cable of Milwaukee having lately confiscated France's home run in these columns. Boone came out to inquire and was shown the statute.9 The fuller indictment of his club wants no catwalk: shut out on one hit in the opener, undone by its own gloves in the second game, New York has scored two runs in 18 innings of this series while the Tampa Bay relief corps proper has been needed for but seven of 54 outs. "We've got to get ourselves up off the mat," said Boone.10

The remedy must be found at home, where the arithmetic grants little: clubs up two games to none in a best-of-five have advanced 83 times in 93, and home winners of the first two under the present format 33 times in 36. Game 3 goes Wednesday at eight o'clock at Yankee Stadium, and the pitching is the hosts' best case: Fried, 5-1 at a 1.81 figure in seven career starts against Tampa Bay and sharp against Boston in the Wild Card round, against the veteran Martinez, a first-time All-Star whose club won 22 of his 31 starts and who held New York to three runs across 12 innings in the Bronx this summer. New York took four of six from the Rays at home this season — but the guests have already corked champagne in that building once this autumn, having clinched the East there on the 22nd of September, and the captain Judge, whose exclusion from these rolls this paper recorded Saturday, remains a spectator still.10

News Around the League

THE ARMS DESK: THE DUEL OF AUGUST IS GRANTED A SECOND SITTING — SALE AGAINST YAMAMOTO AT SIX O'CLOCK IN GEORGIA, THE SERIES SQUARE AND THE THIRD GAME, BY THE LONG LEDGER, THE HINGE OF THE WHOLE QUARREL

The engagement this paper's Monday number announced — the aces unsheathed at last — holds for this evening at Truist Park, and it arrives with a rehearsal already in the books. On the 27th of August these same two men met in this same yard and played a 1-0 masterpiece: Chris Sale a five-hit shutout of the Dodgers, Yoshinobu Yamamoto one run across 6 1/3 innings and the loss for his trouble. Sale, 37 years old, finished the summer with the game's third-best figure at 2.16 — a 1.96 mark over his final 24 starts — and opened this October by holding Philadelphia to three runs over 6 1/3 in the Wild Card round; he was held back from the second game because he had recorded the final four outs of the Wild Card clincher. Yamamoto, the reigning hero of the World Series, makes his first appearance of this postseason carrying a 0.87 WHIP, second among all qualified starters.11

The counting-men assign tonight its full weight: in best-of-five series standing one game apiece, the winner of the third has claimed the series 48 times in 67. The bullpens behind the aces are unevenly provisioned — Atlanta has Iglesias, Suarez, and Lee rested but must do without Fuentes and Kerr, both past 40 pitches Sunday, while Los Angeles returns nearly whole, the rookie Sasaki's 36 pitches the lone question. As for the bats: Harris, 8 for 20 this October, carries Atlanta's order; Acuña (3 for 18 without an extra-base hit) and Olson (3 for 19, seven strikeouts) have yet to join him; Freeman, 3 for 7 with a home run in the series, looks repaired; and Baldwin's leadoff blast accounted for the only run Yamamoto allowed in the August meeting. First pitch at six o'clock.11

THE BRINK DESK: MILWAUKEE CARRIES TWO GAMES AND A PLAIN-SPOKEN STARTER TO THE MISSION SHORE — MAY, THE DEADLINE PRIZE WHO CALLS HIS OWN AUTUMN FRANKLY, AGAINST PIVETTA, FIVE MONTHS MENDED, AT HALF PAST NINE

The National's other quarrel resumes at Petco Park with San Diego's season reduced to a single sentence, supplied by the second baseman Cronenworth: "Win-or-go-home games from here on out, so yeah, we have no choice." Milwaukee hands the ball to Dustin May, its highest-priced freight of the Trade Deadline, whose candor has outrun his results — three earned runs over his first 13 Milwaukee innings, then a 1-2, 7.61 slide across his final eight turns, of which the man himself testified: "It sucks to be sucking right now." The club's wager rests on the fuller ledger: a 3.14 figure in 16 career games against the Friars, and a 1.23 mark in his three starts against them this season. San Diego answers with Nick Pivetta, who lost nearly five months to a flexor strain and has been excellent since his September return — a 1.64 figure across five starts — and whose ugly career number against Milwaukee, 8.76, traces nearly whole to one rookie afternoon of 2017.12

The arithmetic of relief favors the visitors besides: Milwaukee's bullpen has thrown nine scoreless innings in this series, with Megill, Uribe, and Ashby rested by the travel day and the fresh starters Gasser, Drohan, and Harrison standing behind May should the leash run short. San Diego's one reinforcement is a familiar name — Buehler, restored Monday from the paternity rolls whose visit from the stork this paper entered Sunday, and available in relief. Among the bats, Chourio's 15 career postseason runs batted in stand one shy of Braun's franchise mark, while France has opened this October 7 for 15 — with a fair claim, these columns have conceded, to eight and a home run besides, the roof at American Family Field having ruled otherwise. Milwaukee, it bears noting, won 42 games in come-from-behind fashion this summer, tied for fifth most in the league — and has now added two more in October. First pitch at half past nine.12

THE INQUEST DESK: WAS THE CLOSER SHOWING HIS CARDS? MILLER PLEADS COMMAND, NOT TELLS — AND SAN DIEGO'S MEN OF FILM, ASKED TWICE, DECLINE TWICE TO SAY

No topic buzzed louder at San Diego's off-day workout than whether Mason Miller, in the ninth inning this paper chronicled Monday, was tipping his pitches. The internet's magistrates have produced their exhibits: still images suggesting the closer's hand sat more visible out of the glove on his fastballs, and film of Frelick, leading off second, touching his neck before the 1-2 slider that Chourio declined with the season's composure. "That just seemed like a really confident take," Miller allowed of the pitch, though he holds the larger charge unproven and beside the point: "I just don't think it had anything to do with the walks. I also have a hard time believing I just magically started doing it... If you execute pitches, you're still going to get guys out." The batsman Sánchez, for his part, swore ignorance — "I don't know if he was tipping or not. Seriously, I don't" — while the Milwaukee manager Murphy delivered a connoisseur's lecture on the art itself: "Where they stand, if their mouth is open or closed, eyes are down, head is up... Big breath. Small breath. There's so many ways to give away a pitch." Asked plainly whether his club had something, Murphy observed only that the practice "is happening" in today's game — and no club mid-series ever says more.13

The San Diego manager Stammen, twice invited to deny a tell, twice declined, pleading instead a crew "dedicated to that every single day" — and offered the more prosaic diagnosis: Miller's trouble arrives chiefly in his second inning of work, and the six-out ask may be retired for the balance of the round. Miller himself sees no cause to renovate: "It kind of seems like a bad time to try to change everything, too." The Herald notes merely that he may be handed the ball tonight with the season in his palm, and that October is a poor month for unanswered questions.13

THE AWARDS DESK: TWENTY NAMES POSTED FOR THE AARON PRIZE — A PANEL OF LEGENDS AND THE PUBLIC'S FRANCHISE OPEN THROUGH THE TWELFTH, WITH THE VERDICTS SEALED UNTIL NOVEMBER

The league Monday posted its finalists for the Hank Aaron Award, the honor for each league's finest regular-season batsman, and the Herald reports the ballot as a ballot: winners will be named the 11th of November at the MLB Awards in Las Vegas, and until then no man has won anything. The American's ten: Alonso of Baltimore, Alvarez of Houston, Arozarena of Seattle, Caminero and Díaz of Tampa Bay, Contreras of Boston, Greene of Detroit, Rice of New York, Vargas of Chicago, and Witt of Kansas City. The National's: Abrams of Washington, Bauers of Milwaukee, Crow-Armstrong of Chicago, De La Cruz and Stewart of Cincinnati, Ohtani of Los Angeles — thrice the holder, 2023 through 2025 — Olson of Atlanta, Schwarber of Philadelphia, Tatis of San Diego, and Walker of St. Louis. The electors are a bench of legends — Jeter, Ortiz, Pujols, Griffey, Chipper Jones, Pedro Martínez, Smoltz, Bench, Biggio, and Murray — and the public may cast its own votes through noon of the 12th.14

The reader with one eye on the bracket will note the resonance: eight of the twenty finalists are still at their labors in the Division Series — Caminero, Díaz, Rice, and Vargas in the American's two quarrels, Bauers, Ohtani, Olson, and Tatis in the National's — and three of them, Rice, Vargas, and Caminero, spent Monday evening adding to the testimony, as the columns above attest.14

THE JURISPRUDENCE DESK: ROBERTS REVOKES A BATSMAN'S RIGHT OF APPEAL — PAGES, AMONG THE LEAGUE'S LEAST SUCCESSFUL PETITIONERS, IS TOLD TO TAP HIS HELMET NO MORE

The machine's new jurisprudence, whose first-season audit these columns entered Saturday, has produced its first October disbarment. Andy Pages, the Los Angeles center fielder, spent a challenge in the second inning of the series opener on a 2-2 pitch that the instruments placed 2.6 inches above the bottom of the zone — comfortably a strike — and the manager Roberts has now withdrawn the privilege entirely. "We talked about obviously a lot this year with Andy's success rate or lack thereof," said Roberts. "I did have a conversation today. So, yeah, we've managed that one going forward." The figures argue the manager's side: among 182 batsmen with ten or more challenges this season, Pages ranked 142nd in overturns against expectation while spending the 33rd-most challenges, and after a clubhouse address on the subject during an August losing streak he did not challenge again all summer. Roberts was at pains to call the policy a tailored one — "it's not a one-size-fits-all situation," says he, professing full faith in Betts's eye for the outside corner — and the club at large rated a respectable challenger, its 51 percent success standing tied for eighth. But October, as Philadelphia's game-ending helmet tap lately demonstrated and as this paper then observed, is no month for a losing petition.15

Two contests on the Tuesday tables, and the American League wrote the same sentence twice: the visitor won, the favorite's yard fell silent, and both series now stand two games to none — Chicago over Cleveland, Tampa Bay over New York, each leader needing one. Tonight the National answers with its third chapters, Los Angeles at Atlanta at six o'clock with Sale opposite Yamamoto, and Milwaukee at San Diego at half past nine with a sweep in prospect and a season in the balance. The morrow returns the American to the stage — Cleveland at Chicago at four o'clock, Tampa Bay at New York at eight — with the National's fourth games to follow in the same evening as needed; and beyond stand the pennant rounds, the National's Championship Series opening the eleventh of the month and the American's the twelfth, by the league's forward ledger.2 Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: A SEASON'S PHILOSOPHY, REDEEMED ON THE FORTIETH PITCH — MILWAUKEE PLAYS EIGHT UNTIDY INNINGS, THEN WALKS THE NINTH ALIVE ONE BASE AT A TIME UNTIL CHOURIO, DOWN TO HIS FINAL STRIKE, LINES THE CLOSER MILLER INTO HEARTBREAK: BREWERS 4, PADRES 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 89 · Monday, the Fifth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A SEASON'S PHILOSOPHY, REDEEMED ON THE FORTIETH PITCH — MILWAUKEE PLAYS EIGHT UNTIDY INNINGS, THEN WALKS THE NINTH ALIVE ONE BASE AT A TIME UNTIL CHOURIO, DOWN TO HIS FINAL STRIKE, LINES THE CLOSER MILLER INTO HEARTBREAK: BREWERS 4, PADRES 3

Asked for the evening's last six outs, San Diego's splendid closer retires the eighth in order and then unravels in the ninth — Yelich, the newly anointed captain, walking and stealing second, Frelick climbing out of a one-and-two count, the pinch-hitter Sánchez declining a hundred-and-three-mile fastball a hair beneath the zone to fill the bases — whereupon Chourio, who had failed with these same bases loaded in the seventh, fouls off a hundred and three and a half, spits on the signature slider, and lines a two-run single to center for the first trailing-into-the-last-inning resurrection in the franchise's October annals; King outpitches the debutant Henderson, France drives in two against the yard whose roof robbed him Saturday, five errors litter the ledger, and the Brew Crew flies west two games to none with history offering San Diego ten chances in three-and-ninety

A week ago, asked why this Milwaukee club should fancy itself different from the seven other October entries the Cream City has sent forth in the past eight autumns — every one of them stopped short of the World Series — the center fielder Garrett Mitchell gave the scribes a plain man's answer: "We're in it until the 27th out. This year, even down to the last out, we still have a chance. That feels different." Sunday his club spent eight innings making the prophecy look foolish and one inning making it scripture. The Brewers resembled nothing less than a nine that had won a hundred and three games: the postseason debutant Henderson loosed a costly wild pitch in the first that opened the scoring's door, the gloves committed three errors to tie the season's high, and the order managed but five hits all afternoon. They entered the ninth trailing 3-2 against Mason Miller, who had breezed through the eighth on three batters and returned for a second inning of work — a closer who posted a 1.67 figure this summer with 129 strikeouts, the most any San Diego reliever has ever collected, and who had twice this season been asked for six outs and twice delivered them without blemish.

The ninth began obediently, Mitchell himself grounding out. Then Christian Yelich, Milwaukee's newly anointed captain, worked a walk and stole second for his trouble; Sal Frelick climbed out of a one-and-two count to walk behind him; and after the pinch-hitter Vaughn flied to center — the seven-and-twentieth out of Mitchell's sermon now standing one swing away — Gary Sánchez came cold off the bench and performed an at-bat of the quiet heroic kind, declining a 103.3-mile fastball a hair beneath the zone and then a slider boring in at his hands, and the bases were full. Up stepped Jackson Chourio, two-and-twenty years old, one day removed from becoming the franchise's October home-run king, as this paper recorded yesterday, and two innings removed from grounding out with these same bases loaded in the seventh. Miller came at him with pure fire: three triple-digit fastballs, and the young man stood at his final strike. He fouled off a hundred and three and a half. He let the signature slider dart for the dirt. And on the fortieth pitch of the closer's evening — a fastball at a hundred and one, in a hittable spot — Chourio lined it to center. Cronenworth laid out at second and missed by inches; Merrill came up throwing and was late by half a second; Yelich and Frelick crossed, 41,683 shook the yard, and Milwaukee had a 4-3 verdict in a game it began the ninth losing — the first such last-inning resurrection in all the franchise's postseason history, and its third October walk-off, joining Moustakas's in 2018 and Morgan's in 2011. The fates, ever fond of a flourish, had arranged for Nyjer Morgan himself to throw one of the evening's ceremonial first pitches. "We're a team that never backs down," said Chourio. "I knew that he was going to come at me with the fastball at some point, so mentally I was just making sure that I was prepared for that."

The lawful innings beforehand had belonged, narrowly, to the visitors. Michael King gave five innings of three-hit, one-run work with six strikeouts, out-pitching Henderson, who surrendered two runs across five frames in his October baptism; Ty France — the same man whose apparent home run the roof confiscated Saturday, as these columns told — singled home runs in the first and the seventh by way of answer, and San Diego led 3-1 in the seventh. The afternoon's untidiness kept the ledger close: five errors between the clubs, three of them Milwaukee's, and two charged to Cronenworth on a single seventh-inning play that let the hosts back within one. Thus was the stage dressed, and thus did a bullpen built precisely for this month hand back a game the Padres had all but banked.

In a clubhouse quiet as a reading room, the closer declined every extenuation. "I didn't do my job today," said Miller. "The cardinal rule is you don't beat yourself. I beat myself today. A base hit with nobody on doesn't win them the game. A base hit after you walked the bases loaded does." The ledger he leaves behind is stern: clubs down two games to none in a best-of-five have come through but ten times in three-and-ninety tryings, and none since the Yankees of 2017. San Diego's consolations are genuine — both games here were settled by a single run, the Friars won three-and-fifty of three-and-eighty at their own yard this year counting two October victories over the Cubs, and the manager Stammen vows the ground will be defended: "We like where we are when we play at home." But Milwaukee flies west with two victories and a two-and-twenty-year-old who slashed .291/.351/.487 this summer, authored the third straight twenty-and-twenty campaign to open a career — a feat previously belonging only to Julio Rodríguez and Bobby Witt Jr. — and now owns the two loudest hits of this October. Game Three goes Tuesday night at half past nine, Eastern time, at Petco Park. "The series isn't over," said Miller, and he is right; it merely leans.

The Postseason Card

THE PLAN WAS PATIENCE, AND PATIENCE THROWS A HUNDRED MILES THE HOUR — KERR OPENS WITHOUT BLEMISH A SECOND TIME, THE BOY FUENTES CLAIMS ELEVEN OF THE LAST TWELVE OUTS, AND HARRIS FINISHES A HOME RUN SHY OF OCTOBER'S SECOND CYCLE AS THE TOMAHAWK NINE SQUARE THE SERIES: BRAVES 3, DODGERS 2

Weiss holds Sale back for full strength and is vindicated twice over — Kerr giving two and two-thirds scoreless three days after a seven-and-forty-pitch night, and the one-and-twenty-year-old Fuentes pouring four-seamers at 99.4 miles the hour across three and two-thirds innings of one-run relief; Snell, rusted by a fortnight's idleness, walks five in three and two-thirds and is lifted at his ninetieth pitch, Dubón cashes the bases-full passes in the first, Harris triples on a sliced sweeper the instruments valued at .016 and scores the decider on Bubic's wild pitch, and Muncy's two-out thunder in the ninth arrives a run short; the aces come off the shelf Tuesday at six at Truist Park, Sale against Yamamoto, with the road split favoring Atlanta thirty times in nine-and-forty under the present format

The manager Weiss spent Saturday night explaining why a fatigued Chris Sale would not pitch Sunday — "We want full-strength Chris Sale. I know him at 80 percent is really good, but that's what it came down to" — and spent Sunday night being proven entirely right. His second consecutive bullpen game ran like a railroad timetable. Ray Kerr, opening for the second time in four days and three days removed from a seven-and-forty-pitch evening against Philadelphia, gave two and two-thirds scoreless innings with four strikeouts, at one point surrendering a leadoff double to Rojas and deliberately pitching around Betts to claim the left-on-left argument with Ohtani. Holmes lasted five batters and gave Freeman's leadoff homer in the fourth — the first baseman's first extra-base hit since the second of September — but Lee tidied the fourth for the victory, Suarez escaped a two-on, none-out crisis in the fifth in just his fourth appearance since the elbow began complaining in late June, and then came the revelation. Didier Fuentes, one-and-twenty years old, poured four-seamers averaging 99.4 miles the hour — two full ticks above his summer figure — across three and two-thirds innings of one-run relief, claiming eleven of the final twelve outs and touching 99 or better four times in the ninth. "I couldn't believe he came back out there for the ninth, but he did and he was still chucking 100," testified Olson. Muncy's two-out blast off the youngster was the only dent, and Iglesias retired De Paula on a popup for the save.

The runs the relay protected were largely the work of one Georgian. Michael Harris II — whose first-inning thunderclap decided Thursday's Wild Card finale, as these columns told — went 3-for-5 and finished a home run shy of what would have been but the second cycle in all postseason history, Brock Holt's of 2018 standing alone. His fifth-inning triple was a thing of fortune honestly collected: an 86-mile sweeper off the plate, sliced away from Hernández, who broke sideways and lost it — the instruments valued the ball at .016 of expected average — and Harris legged it to third, whence Bubic's wild pitch brought him home with the lead. His double cashed Olson for insurance in the seventh, making him the fifth Brave ever to triple and double in a single postseason game, after Acuña, DeRosa, Lemke, and Gowdy of 1914. The boy who watched the 2021 champions from the Truist Park stands now carries their successors. "There seems to always be unsung heroes in the postseason," said Weiss. "Tonight it was Michael Harris."

Los Angeles, by contrast, beat itself with a thousand small cuts. Snell, who had thrown but five innings on six-and-ninety pitches in the fortnight and a half since his groin tightened in mid-September, walked five in three and two-thirds — two of them loading the first-inning bases for Dubón's two-out single — and was lifted at his ninetieth pitch. "He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game," said Roberts. The order went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position, stranded seven, and has now scored all seven of its series runs by the home run. The champions' consolations were Díaz's electric sixth, entered in the columns above, and the knowledge that their rotation remains the deepest in the field. "So now it's a three-game series," said Roberts — one that resumes Tuesday at six o'clock at Truist Park with the aces unsheathed at last, Sale against Yamamoto, and Mahle to follow in Wednesday's fourth game. The counting-men give the side that splits on the road and goes home thirty series in nine-and-forty under the present arrangement; Weiss, for his part, keeps the accounting simpler: "Every starter on their staff is a Cy Young guy. It doesn't get any easier, but I like the fact that we go back home even and we have Chris Sale."

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: CLEVELAND'S OCTOBER NARROWS TO A SINGLE EVENING — WILLIAMS AND HIS TWO-HUNDRED-AND-FORTY-EIGHT STRIKEOUTS TAKE THE BALL AT FIVE O'CLOCK, AGAINST A SOUTH SIDE RELAY OF KAY AND BURKE, WITH THE HOSTS ONE DEFEAT FROM A TWO-GAMES HOLE

The particulars this paper left open yesterday are now filled in. For this evening's second chapter on Lake Erie's shore, the manager Venable confirms the South Siders will repeat the method that shut Cleveland out in the opener: the left-hander Anthony Kay opens against the top of the order — Kwan, Ramírez, DeLauter, two lefties and a switch-man — and Sean Burke, the staff's ace by every figure, follows in bulk. The assignment could scarcely suit him better: Burke went 2-0 against Cleveland this summer at a 1.04 figure, one-and-twenty strikeouts in seventeen innings and a third, and carries a lifetime 2.57 mark at Progressive Field; across the season he struck out 185 in 172 and a third. "I dreamed of the World Series when I dreamed of playoff starts," says he of the unglamorous role. "So whatever's going to get us to the World Series, I'm all in on doing that." The heroes of Saturday may even reappear, Venable declaring both Smith and Taylor candidates according to feel, aided by Sunday's idleness and another off day Tuesday.

Cleveland answers with its heaviest remaining artillery: Gavin Williams, second in all the game with 248 strikeouts and author of eleven starts of ten strikeouts or better, the most in the majors. The hosts' predicament wants no embroidery — shut out on three hits in the opener, they stand one defeat from a two-games hole with the series then removing to Chicago. The manager Vogt declines the panic: "It was one game. We've lost a lot of games this year, and we've bounced back the next day... We still have a great opportunity ahead of us to even the series tomorrow and go to Chicago with a chance to win it." First pitch at five o'clock.

THE ARMS DESK: AT THE DOME AT EIGHT, THE ROAD WARRIOR AND HIS NEW CURVEBALL MEET SEPTEMBER'S ADOPTED KING — SCHLITTLER AGAINST PERALTA, WITH NEW YORK WANTING THE SPLIT AND ONE HIT TO ITS NAME

The young right-hander Schlittler, named in these columns yesterday for tonight's assignment, arrives at Tropicana Field as the finest road pitcher in the game — an 8-2 account and a 1.16 figure across seventeen travelling starts this season, both tops in the majors, with a .153 average against — and with a new weapon besides. The game's foremost fastball merchant, who threw his three fastball shapes nine-and-eighty times in every hundred pitches this summer, the highest such rate among all starters, unveiled a power curve in earnest against Boston last week: two-and-thirty of them, a career high, drawing eight empty swings and accounting for four of his ten strikeouts. The scribes already presume him the American's Cy Young choice; that ballot is counted in November, and this paper will enter the verdict when the official rolls do. His catcher Wells states tonight's business plainly: "Hopefully get to their guy."

Their guy is Freddy Peralta, got from the Mets in August and transformed by the crossing: the American's Pitcher of the Month for September on a 5-0, 0.79 run across his final six starts, with a 1.69 figure in four home turns beneath the dome. "Everything changed when I got traded," says the right-hander. "I've been treated here as a king." He inherits a crowd still roaring from Saturday's one-hitter and an order that held New York to a single safety in the opener — the fewest of the franchise's four hundred and forty-seven postseason games, as this paper recorded. First pitch at eight o'clock.

THE BULLPEN DESK: THE TRUMPETS SOUND IN THE SIXTH INNING, OF ALL PLACES — DÍAZ, IN HIS LOS ANGELES OCTOBER DEBUT, THROWS HIS HARDEST PITCH IN TWO YEARS, AND THE CHAMPIONS NAME IT THEIR SILVER LINING

When the trumpets of "Narco" rang through Dodger Stadium Sunday evening, they announced not the ninth inning but the sixth — and Edwin Díaz, the closer signed at $69 million over three winters to anchor the champions' late innings, delivered the finest frame of his disrupted season in a losing cause. Three up and three down: Riley frozen on consecutive sliders for a three-pitch strikeout, the pinch-hitter Yastrzemski blown away at 100.8 miles the hour — Díaz's hardest pitch since the fourth game of the 2024 Division Series — and Baldwin's fly ball to end a twelve-pitch performance that touched a hundred three times, his most in any outing since September of 2024. "Try to find some silver linings — that was a silver lining and certainly a positive," ruled the manager Roberts, whose club has now seen every Atlanta reliever save the rookie Ritchie. The pitcher himself was less circumspect: "That's why I came here — to help this team win and pitch in big spots. I want to keep getting the ball and doing my job." The Herald observes that a bullpen's repairs, like a batsman's, tend to be tested soonest in Georgia.

THE ALMANAC DESK: BEFORE CHICAGO AND CLEVELAND QUARRELED FOR A PENNANT, THEY CONSPIRED TO INVENT THE LEAGUE THEY QUARREL IN — A REMINISCENCE OF BAN JOHNSON, THE SPIDERS' DREADFUL SUMMER, AND A BLUFF CALLED IN A MILWAUKEE HOTEL

As the Central rivals contest their Game Two this evening, the league's historians supply a pleasing symmetry: the American League itself was conjured largely out of these two cities. In the autumn of 1899, Ban Johnson — a former sporting editor running the minor Western League — renamed his circuit the American League and resolved to challenge the National's monopoly, exhorting his owners to "fight them with fire, gentlemen!" Cleveland lay open for the taking, the National's Spiders having just completed a season of 20 victories against 134 defeats, the worst ever entered in the books — a mark lately challenged, the Herald notes with a diplomatic cough, by the 121 losses of the 2024 White Sox — and Johnson moved the Grand Rapids franchise there under the purses of Somers and Kilfoyle. The league was formally incorporated at the Republican House Hotel in Milwaukee on the fifth of March, 1900; the National's threatened counter-invasion proved, in the end, nothing more than a bluff.

Chicago required delicacy of another kind: the National's man Hart permitted the upstart club his league's cast-off name "White Stockings" on the condition that the word "Chicago" form no official part of the title. The new league declared itself major by 1901, and its first big-league game, fittingly, matched these very antagonists — Chicago against Cleveland, the 24th of April, 1901, at South Side Park, the White Stockings prevailing 8-2 on their way to the new league's first pennant. The peace of 1903 brought the first World Series, and the rest is the national pastime as we know it. A century and a quarter on, the argument resumes at five o'clock.

Two contests only on the Monday tables, but each a chapter heading: Milwaukee stands two games to none over San Diego, its consecutive one-run escapes achieved by roof and by rally, while Atlanta and Los Angeles square at one apiece with the aces Sale and Yamamoto booked opposite for Tuesday at six. Today the American League takes the stage back — Chicago at Cleveland at five o'clock, New York at Tampa Bay at eight, the burgling South Siders and the top-seeded Rays each a victory from commanding their quarrels outright. Tuesday carries the National's third games besides, Los Angeles at Atlanta at six and Milwaukee at San Diego at half past nine; and the pennant rounds stand ready beyond, the National's Championship Series opening the eleventh of the month and the American's the twelfth, by the league's forward ledger. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE LOUDEST ROOM IN FLORIDA GOES QUIET ONE BATTER AT A TIME — RASMUSSEN CARRIES A NO-HITTER INTO THE EIGHTH, THE LONE NEW YORK HIT DIES AT THIRD BASE ON A PERFECT RELAY, AND ARANDA'S SOLITARY THUNDERCLAP IS THE WHOLE OF THE SCORING: RAYS 1, YANKEES 0
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 88 · Sunday, the Fourth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 4 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE LOUDEST ROOM IN FLORIDA GOES QUIET ONE BATTER AT A TIME — RASMUSSEN CARRIES A NO-HITTER INTO THE EIGHTH, THE LONE NEW YORK HIT DIES AT THIRD BASE ON A PERFECT RELAY, AND ARANDA'S SOLITARY THUNDERCLAP IS THE WHOLE OF THE SCORING: RAYS 1, YANKEES 0

Ten strikeouts, three-and-twenty swinging strikes, and three-and-twenty of six-and-twenty men retired — the right-hander becomes but the seventh pitcher of the Modern Era to carry a no-hit bid through seven and two-thirds October innings, the first since Aníbal Sánchez in 2019, while the Yankees' single safety is the fewest of their four hundred and forty-seven postseason games; Cole gives five creditable innings and is beaten by a changeup, Wells breaks up the history with two out in the eighth and is thrown out stretching for his trouble, and the Sunshine State's first playoff victory since 2021 arrives before a sold-out and thunderous dome — with Game Two Monday at eight o'clock and the captain Judge, by the roster's verdict, nowhere on the rolls

The loudest room in Florida went quiet one batter at a time. Drew Rasmussen, whom his own pitching instructor Snyder calls "the industry standard," took the ball for Game One of the Division Series before a sold-out Tropicana Field — 40,542 souls, the towels already whirling — and for seven innings and two-thirds he permitted the famous New York order nothing at all: no hit of any denomination, two passes his only lapses, fifteen men retired in one unbroken procession. Ten strikeouts he collected, and three-and-twenty swinging strikes, the most any Tampa Bay man has drawn in a postseason game; of six-and-twenty batters faced he retired three-and-twenty. The scribes certify him the seventh pitcher of the Modern Era to carry a no-hit bid through seven and two-thirds innings of an October game, and the first since Aníbal Sánchez turned the trick for Washington in the 2019 Championship Series. "My heart rate was at a thousand beats per minute," the right-hander confessed afterward. "I was just trying to execute one pitch at a time."

The history was broken, and then punished. Austin Wells, with two out in the eighth, lined a double down the right-field line — whereupon, seeing the stop sign too late, he charged for third and was thrown out by a relay of textbook beauty, Mesa to Walls to Caminero, the lone New York baserunner of consequence erased in the act of overreaching. "Just obviously not a good decision there," ruled the manager Boone. One hit was the evening's entire New York produce — the fewest in the four hundred and forty-seven postseason games the franchise has played, a ledger that reaches back to the days of Ruth — and when Baker struck out two in a clean ninth, the Rays had their first playoff victory since the opening game of the 2021 Division Series, by the severe and ancient score of 1-0.

The run itself was a single stroke of thunder: Jonathan Aranda, in the third, turned on a Gerrit Cole changeup and deposited it in the right-center seats. Cole was otherwise creditable — five innings, five hits, one run, five strikeouts, in his first postseason start since the 2024 World Series — and his bullpen gave nothing behind him. "You've got to tip your cap," was the sentiment of the visiting clubhouse, though Cole himself framed it as a fighter would: "They're going to land some blows. You've got to take blows in the postseason, and you've got to dish them out, too." The hosts, for their part, have now won each of Rasmussen's last thirteen starts, and the man's career ledger against New York — five victories against two at a 1.81 figure — reads like a standing indictment. His manager Cash, who lately compared the fellow's preparation to Roy Halladay's, declined to retract: "I've said a lot of dumb things in my life. That one was not."

So the top seed leads, one game to none, and the arithmetic the Herald entered yesterday now works for Tampa Bay: clubs that take the opener of a best-of-five have advanced 116 times in 160 tryings, and the home winners of Game One under the present format 42 of 56. Game Two goes Monday at eight o'clock beneath the same dome, the young right-hander Schlittler taking the ball for New York — and the Yankees, who must in all likelihood solve Rasmussen once more before this series is through, will attempt it without their captain, the roster's verdict on Judge being rendered at last and reported in the columns below. "It's a tall order," allowed the first baseman Rice. "I think we're built for it."

The Postseason Card

SEVEN-AND-TWENTY INNINGS OF OCTOBER AND NOT ONE OF THEM PLAYED FROM BEHIND — MURAKAMI'S FOUR-HUNDRED-AND-FORTY-FOOT THUNDERCLAP AND A FOUR-INNING SAVE OF THE ANTIQUE SCHOOL SHUT OUT THE FOREST CITY NINE: WHITE STOCKINGS 3, CLEVELANDS 0

Five Chicago arms braid a three-hitter at Progressive Field, the rookie Smith walks the bases full and is rescued twice by routine fly balls, and young Grant Taylor — two days removed from a four-and-fifty-pitch career high — claims the final twelve outs with six strikeouts, closing the ninth by fanning three men on eleven pitches; the visitors have not trailed in this postseason's seven-and-twenty innings, Messick wears a loss his six strikeouts scarcely deserved, and Game Two goes Monday at five o'clock with the strikeout king Williams standing between Cleveland and a two-games hole

The question on the South Side is no longer whether the White Stockings will win October games; it is whether they will ever consent to trail in one. Saturday's 3-0 verdict at Progressive Field — a three-hit shutout administered to the division champions in their own yard — ran Chicago's postseason account to seven-and-twenty innings without once standing behind, and the counting-men certify the deeper figure: the lead held at the end of four-and-twenty of those innings, the most in the first three games of any postseason in the franchise's annals, and matched in the last twenty years only by the 2019 Yankees and the 2017 Dodgers.

The decisive blow belonged, as it so often has this remarkable season, to Munetaka Murakami. The Japanese first baseman, whose arrival re-energized the whole enterprise, met a Parker Messick offering in the fourth — Vargas aboard by a single — and sent it a Statcast-certified four hundred and forty feet for the game's first two runs. Colson Montgomery's double cashed Teel in the seventh for the third, and that was the whole of the scoring, for the Chicago relay required no more. The rookie Hagen Smith walked the bases full with two out in the third and was rescued by Hudson's routine fly ball; a fourth-inning crisis died the same polite death against Kay; and then came the antique theater. Grant Taylor, two days removed from a career-high four-and-fifty pitches in Houston, took the ball for the final four innings and never gave it back — six strikeouts, the last three of them administered to Martínez, Lowe, and Bazzana on eleven pitches in the ninth, a four-inning save of the old school. "That's what playoff baseball is about," said the manager Venable. "Your big dogs going out there and making big plays."

Cleveland, which had not played in a week, mustered three hits and twelve strikeouts against the procession, and Messick — six strikeouts in four and a third, undone by the one swing — wore a loss his line scarcely deserved. The fourteenth meeting of the summer's closest neighbors thus goes to the guests, who took seven of thirteen from these same Clevelands in the regular campaign and now stand two victories from a first Championship Series since 2005. Game Two goes Monday at five o'clock on Lake Erie's shore, and the hosts hand the ball to Gavin Williams, whose 248 strikeouts led the American League — with Burke expected to answer in some capacity for Chicago, and the series guaranteed in any event to call at Rate Field come Wednesday.

THE CHEERS HE ORDERED ARRIVE ON SCHEDULE, AND IN HUNDRED-DEGREE HEAT — SKUBAL CARVES SIX INNINGS IN HIS FIRST HOME OCTOBER START WHILE ATLANTA'S BULLPEN-DOOR ROULETTE COMES UP EMPTY: BOYS IN BLUE 5, BRAVES 3

The left-hander twice crowned the American League's finest surrenders a leadoff single and then retires fifteen straight, Teoscar Hernández, Tucker, and Muncy supply three home runs off the fourth and fifth Atlanta arms, and Albies' two-run answer in the ninth arrives two innings too late; Dodd's three scoreless innings as opener are squandered by a bullpen stripped of its high-leverage men, Weiss declares himself unworried with Sale still undecided for Game Two this very evening at eight o'clock against Snell, and the champions' arithmetic now reads one game to none with their two best arms yet unused

The cheers Tarik Skubal requested in these columns yesterday were delivered on schedule, 50,194 strong, in heat that touched one hundred degrees at the first pitch. The left-hander — twice crowned the American League's finest arm in his Detroit years, and making at last the first home postseason start of his life — surrendered a leadoff single to Baldwin and then retired fifteen Atlantas in unbroken succession, finishing with six innings of two-hit, one-run, seven-strikeout work, Murphy's sixth-inning solo blast the only blemish on the afternoon. The tailored reasoning that gave him the ball over Yamamoto, which this paper entered Saturday, wanted no further argument by evening.

Atlanta's half of the ledger was the mirror and the misfortune. Dylan Dodd, the opener, gave three scoreless innings that deserved coronation — whereupon the roulette of the bullpen door, spun of necessity with Fuentes and Suarez both spent from the Wild Card round, came up empty twice. Mederos, summoned for the fourth, was met by Teoscar Hernández's two-run thunder; Smith-Shawver, asked for the middle innings, surrendered Tucker's two-run blast and Muncy's solo in the sixth; and 5-1 was the account when Albies — now four for twelve this October with two home runs and a triple — answered with two aboard in the ninth off Scott, two innings too late for the difference. Phillips recorded the final out with the tying men in the on-deck circle's imagination only. "I don't have any worries about having enough pitching," declared the manager Weiss afterward. "We've got plenty of pitching." The Herald, which has chronicled the invalid rolls that swallowed Schwellenbach, Waldrep, Strider, López, Elder, and Pérez, admires the confidence and withholds the endorsement.

The second chapter comes this very evening at eight o'clock at Dodger Stadium, and the stakes are the series' whole shape: clubs that seize the first two games of a best-of-five have advanced nine-and-eighty times in a hundred. The hosts send Blake Snell, whose strikeout rate stood sixth among all starters this summer despite a season of but nine starts; Atlanta had not, by press time, decided whether Sale — five-and-ninety pitches Tuesday and one-and-twenty more Thursday — takes the ball or waits for Georgia, with Holmes and the rookie Ritchie the alternatives, and Lane Thomas restored to the October rolls for his first start since the seventh of September. The champions, meanwhile, hold Yamamoto in the holster for Game Three — an abundance their president Friedman says improves his quality of life, and his counterpart Anthopoulos can only envy.

THE ROOF ITSELF ENLISTS WITH THE HOME NINE — FRANCE'S WOULD-BE THUNDERCLAP STRIKES A CABLE IN THE NINTH AND FALLS INTO CHOURIO'S GLOVE, AND THE MILWAUKEES SURVIVE THE OPENER BY THE WIDTH OF A TRUSS: MILWAUKEES 3, SAN DIEGOS 2

Misiorowski opens with the fastest pitch October has ever recorded at 104.8 miles the hour and is nonetheless wrung dry in four innings by thirty foul balls, Chourio's game-tying blast makes him at two-and-twenty the franchise's October home-run king, and Contreras — benched for loafing a week ago — trots a go-ahead homer home in the seventh; then, with one on and one out in the ninth, France launches a drive the Padres swear was leaving the yard until a roof cable swats it down for the strangest out of the autumn, the challenge is denied, and Game Two goes this afternoon at four o'clock, King against Henderson

The Herald has entered many verdicts in its columns; rarely one co-signed by the building. With Milwaukee ahead 3-2 in the ninth Saturday night, one San Diego man aboard and one out, Ty France launched a towering drive toward the left-field corner — a blow the batsman himself pronounced gone, and which two Milwaukee coaches, consulting their private camera angles, privately agreed was staying fair — whereupon it struck a cable on the roof of American Family Field, changed its mind in midair, and settled into Jackson Chourio's glove for the second out. The ground rules, recited by the umpire Mahrley at the lineup exchange that very afternoon to general laughter, were unambiguous: struck in fair territory and caught, the ball is an out. San Diego's challenge, pleading foul-territory contact, was denied upon review. "I came in here and said, 'Incredible home-field advantage,'" testified the Milwaukee coach Erickson. "That's the advantage you get when you win 103 games." The manager Murphy assigned the intervention higher authority still: "'Ueck' reached up there and knocked that ball down." The counting-men note the drive left the bat at nine-and-forty degrees of launch, an angle that has cleared a fence but ten times in the whole tracking era — and note besides that this is the second San Diego homer confiscated by architecture this season, Bogaerts having lost one to the Tropicana catwalks in August.

The lawful baseball preceding the miracle was itself worth the admission. Misiorowski, the young ace who led all the game in earned runs this summer, opened the evening at 104.8 miles the hour to Tatis — the fastest pitch October has recorded since the tracking began, wresting the mark from San Diego's own Mason Miller — and was nonetheless wrung dry inside four innings, the Padres fouling off thirty pitches in that span, the most ever counted in a postseason game's first four frames, and cashing two second-inning runs on a parade of one-out singles and a fielder's choice misplayed at first. "His velo dropped five miles per hour almost in the second inning," allowed the manager Murphy of the early hook. The order answered for him: Chourio's two-run blast in the third — which made him, at two-and-twenty years, the franchise's leader with five October home runs — squared the account, and in the seventh William Contreras, benched a week ago for declining to run out a grounder, turned on Morejon's offering and was granted the rare luxury of a trot. Five relievers carried the rest, Hall escaping a bases-full seventh and Megill striking out Tatis with the tying run at third before presiding over the ninth's architecture.

So the club that hit the fewest home runs in the National League won on two of them, and the hottest team in baseball fell by the width of a truss. Game Two goes this very afternoon at four o'clock beneath the same roof: Michael King, whose career October figure stands at 2.05 and who carried a no-hitter into the seventh against Chicago in the Wild Card round, against the composed young right-hander Logan Henderson, eleven victories against three at a 2.47 figure, who has never in three-and-twenty career starts allowed more than three runs. The San Diegos could scarcely ask a better man for a must-have game; neither, the Milwaukees would answer, could they.

News Around the League

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE, THE VERDICT: JUDGE IS LEFT OFF THE DIVISION SERIES ROLLS — SEVENTEEN DAYS OF ARGUING WITH THE ARITHMETIC END WITH THE CALF UNPERSUADED, AND NEW YORK OPENS OCTOBER'S SECOND ROUND WITHOUT ITS THREE-TIME MOST VALUABLE

The case this paper has followed since the calf first gave way on the sixteenth of September is closed, and the verdict went against the plaintiff: Aaron Judge's name does not appear on the Yankees' roster for the Division Series against Tampa Bay, the wire's correspondents reporting the decision Saturday before the opener. The docket of his rehabilitation was thorough to the last — the platelet injection, the rounds of live batting practice in the Bronx and at Somerset, Friday's early workout across the bay, the shirt reading "No time like October" — but the one exercise the captain never completed was the running of the bases, and the moderate strain of the soleus, which ordinarily asks three weeks, declined in the end to be hurried into seventeen days.

The consequence was visible at once in Saturday's batting order, which carried no Judge and mustered one hit, and the fuller measure of it is entered in the game account above. The Herald, which has reported each hearing of this case in its turn, enters the verdict without garnish: the finest batsman of his generation will watch the Division Series from the rail, and New York's October now rests upon the rotation it spent all summer touting and an order that must discover its thunder elsewhere.

THE ROSTER DESK: A DEBUTANT OF THREE WEEKS' STANDING CRACKS THE CHAMPIONS' OCTOBER ROLLS, MUSGROVE KEEPS HIS SEAT IN SAN DIEGO, AND BUEHLER REPAIRS TO THE PATERNITY LIST AS THE FIRST STORK OF THE POSTSEASON CALLS

The Division Series rosters published Saturday carried their small surprises. In Los Angeles, the champions found room for Josue De Paula, the young outfielder whose major-league debut came but three weeks ago — a bold entry on an October roll, and a mark of the esteem the club's counting-men hold for the bat. In San Diego, the Friars stood entirely pat from their Wild Card sweep, Joe Musgrove keeping his seat among the arms — though Walker Buehler begins the series on the paternity list, the autumn's first visit from the stork, with his return to the rolls expected when the series removes to California. Milwaukee, for its part, restored the bat of Andrew Vaughn from the invalid rolls Friday, and he promptly delivered a pinch single in the opener.

THE DISCIPLINE DESK: TWO FIFTY-SIX-GAME SENTENCES HANDED DOWN UNDER THE MINOR-LEAGUE DRUG STATUTES — THE WASHINGTON CATCHER RIVERO AND THE FREE AGENT PÉREZ TAKEN UP FOR THE PERFORMANCE-ENHANCING ARTICLE

While eight clubs quarreled over the pennants, the league's constabulary was at its quieter work: Francisco Rivero, a catcher of the Washington organization, and Raudi Pérez, a pitcher presently of no club at all, were each suspended six-and-fifty games following positive tests for a performance-enhancing substance under the minor leagues' drug programs. The Herald reports the sentences as the wire gives them, without editorial — observing only that the game's October stage and its October woodshed operate, as ever, on the same calendar.

The Sunday tables, then — four contests entered, the four Division Series each one game old, and the form chart's first verdict is unanimous in one particular: the opener went to the home nine in three yards of four, Chicago's road burglary at Cleveland the lone exception, and every Game One winner now enjoys the arithmetic this paper printed yesterday in prospect — 116 of 160 best-of-five leaders have gone through. The second chapters divide between today and tomorrow: San Diego at Milwaukee at four o'clock and Atlanta at Los Angeles at eight this afternoon and evening, then Monday the American League's turn, Chicago at Cleveland at five and New York at Tampa Bay at eight — the latter to be contested, by Saturday's roster verdict, without the captain Judge. The Herald's columns will carry each in its fullest measure. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Third of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 87 · Saturday, the Third of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the first pitch of the Division Series — four Game Ones this very day, beginning at one o'clock on Lake Erie's shore (Saturday, the 3rd of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE QUIET DAY PASSES AND THE FOUR QUARRELS OPEN IN A SINGLE AFTERNOON — CHICAGO AT CLEVELAND AT ONE, ATLANTA AT LOS ANGELES AT FOUR, NEW YORK AT TAMPA BAY AT HALF PAST SIX, SAN DIEGO AT MILWAUKEE AT HALF PAST EIGHT

The calm this paper forecast arrived on schedule: Friday passed without a contest anywhere in the land, the travel day observed by all eight survivors, and today the October proper begins at the fuller measure. The card, verified against the league's forward ledger, reads thus: the Pale Hose call at Cleveland at one o'clock, Hagen Smith (3-3, a 1.29 figure) against Parker Messick (12-9, 2.56), the rookie left-handers squared off; Atlanta calls at Los Angeles at four, the hosts sending Tarik Skubal (12-7, 2.72) against a visiting starter yet unnamed; the Yankees call at Tampa Bay at half past six, Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61) against Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67); and the Friars call at Milwaukee at half past eight, Robbie Ray (13-8, 3.59) against Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80), the leader of all the game in earned runs.

The second chapters follow hard upon: Sunday carries San Diego at Milwaukee at four o'clock and Atlanta at Los Angeles at eight; Monday, Chicago at Cleveland at five and New York at Tampa Bay at eight; and Tuesday the National League quarrels remove to Atlanta and San Diego. Four series, every one a best-of-five, and the particulars of each are entered below — the Herald having spent the idle Friday at the armory, as a paper should.

THE CENTRAL QUARREL, FOURTEENTH MEETING: A DIVISION SETTLED BY ONE GAME RESUMES ON LAKE ERIE'S SHORE — ROOKIE LEFT-HANDER AGAINST ROOKIE LEFT-HANDER AT ONE O'CLOCK, AND THE SUMMER'S LEDGER GIVES THE GUESTS THE EDGE

The thirteen meetings of the summer were not enough to settle the argument, so Cleveland and the Pale Hose will hold a fourteenth with everything at stake. The division fell to the Lake Erie men by a single game, 85 victories against 84, and by the narrowest of mechanisms — a three-game set taken at Progressive Field in the middle of September, the lead changing hands for the last time. Yet the season's ledger between them belongs to Chicago, seven games to six, the aggregate scoring 58 runs to 57; seven of the thirteen were settled by a single run, and four ended in walk-offs. Chicago held at least a share of first place for six-and-ninety days, Cleveland for nine-and-eighty. "Obviously we know Chicago really well," allows the Cleveland manager Vogt. "A really good team offensively. They've got a lot of power and they match up really well with us pitching-wise."

The pitching opens with a curiosity the deadball fathers never saw: two rookie left-handers, each his club's chosen man. Messick, whose Game One assignment this paper entered Friday, has faced the Chicagos four times this summer at a 2.81 figure, nine-and-twenty strikeouts against five passes in five-and-twenty innings and two-thirds. Smith, for his part, makes his second start of the week — three scoreless innings in Tuesday's Wild Card victory over Houston — and has held Cleveland to a 3.18 figure across his innings against them; three or four efficient frames would seem his ration, after which the manager Venable may call on young Grant Taylor and the rest of a bullpen that shut Houston out across the final five frames of the clincher. The South Side club used an opener one-and-thirty times this season, the most in the majors, and with idle days Sunday and Tuesday, Venable declares both Smith and Taylor may appear in any of the first three games. The first October meeting of the Central neighbors in their whole long acquaintance, and it could scarcely be drawn tighter.

THE EXPECTATION OVERTURNED IN CHAVEZ RAVINE: SKUBAL, NOT YAMAMOTO, TAKES THE BALL FOR GAME ONE — WHILE ATLANTA, ITS ROTATION ON THE INVALID ROLLS, DECLINES TO NAME A STARTER AT ALL

The expectation this paper recorded Friday is overturned: the Angelenos hand Game One not to Yamamoto but to Tarik Skubal, the left-hander acquired at the summer's Trade Deadline. The reasoning is a tailored one — the Atlanta order struggled against southpaws all season — and the price is acknowledged: Yamamoto, who last autumn threw consecutive complete games in the Championship Series and the World Series and then closed out the seventh game of the latter on no rest at all, was the only arrangement that returned the Japanese right-hander twice on regular rest in a five-game series. "I loved delivering that message," said the manager Roberts of informing Skubal. "I don't always get to deliver good messages, and that was a good one." The pitcher learned his assignment on the five-and-twentieth of September, walking off the mound after seven scoreless innings in San Francisco. His October credentials want nothing: a 2.04 figure across six postseason starts, six-and-fifty strikeouts in nine-and-thirty innings and two-thirds — every one of those starts made on the road, in his Detroit years. Saturday, at last, a home crowd. "Usually when I walk out onto the field in a playoff game, it's received with a lot of boos," said Skubal. "I'm excited to get some cheers in there for us."

Atlanta, by the sharpest contrast, arrives with no starter named at all, its rotation depleted exactly as this paper entered Friday: Sale unavailable before Sunday's second game, Mahle before Tuesday's third, Pérez — on the invalid rolls with the low back since the first of September — likewise barred until Game Three. The likeliest arrangement asks Grant Holmes, who threw but two innings in Thursday's clincher, for the early frames, perhaps behind the left-hander Suter as an opener. The handedness will also arrange the home order: against left-handed pitching the champions lead off Betts rather than Ohtani, and Skubal's presence makes the choice for them. Triple-digit heat is in the forecast for the four-o'clock first pitch — the two clubs' first October meeting since the 2021 Championship Series, which Atlanta took on its way to the title, and the hosts' first step toward a third consecutive one.

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE, THIRD HEARING: NEW YORK WEIGHS JUDGE'S NAME FOR THE DIVISION SERIES ROLLS AS THE DEADLINE ARRIVES — THE CALF HAS NOT YET RUN THE BASES, BUT THE SHIRT SAYS 'NO TIME LIKE OCTOBER'

The case this paper has followed since the calf first gave way on the sixteenth of September reached its final hearing Friday at Tropicana Field, where Aaron Judge — dressed for work hours before his teammates arrived, a shirt across his chest reading "No time like October" — awaited the club's verdict on his place on the Division Series roster, due by the evening. The docket of his rehabilitation is thorough: a platelet-poor plasma injection in late September, four turns of live batting practice Monday in the Bronx, further at-bats Wednesday at the Double-A grounds in Somerset, more hitting Thursday, and an early workout Friday across the bay in Tampa. What the captain has not yet done is run the bases, though the manager Boone suggests he may not need to — "sometimes running the bases, they replicate things in other ways," says he, framing the question before the club thus: "Is he going to be available at some point in this series potentially as a player?" The moderate strain of the soleus ordinarily asks three weeks; the three-time Most Valuable has spent seventeen days arguing with the arithmetic.

With or without him, the series wants no garnish. The Yankees and the Sunshine nine have met in October once in all their quarrelsome acquaintance — the 2020 Division Series, played in the neutral yard at San Diego and ended by Brosseau's blast off Chapman — and never once with both home crowds in attendance. Tampa Bay, the American's top seed at 98-64, went 55-26 in its return to the home dome this summer, and celebrated its division title on the Yankee Stadium lawn besides. New York's answer is the man it pays for precisely this assignment: Cole has given the Rays nine earned runs across his last six starts against them, a 2.09 figure. "Every time we play them, it's a tight game, it's a dogfight," says Rasmussen, who takes the ball opposite. The captain himself, whatever the rolls say by game time, put it plainest: "It's going to be a grind the next five games."

THE TOP SEED'S EXAMINATION: MILWAUKEE'S HUNDRED-THREE-WIN SUMMER MEETS THE ONE CLUB THAT SWEPT IT — RAY CHOSEN OVER BUEHLER TO EXPLOIT THE SUDS MEN'S ONE SOFT SPOT, AND MISIOROWSKI ANSWERS WITH THE BEST FIGURES IN BASEBALL

The season's best club takes the field at last tonight, and the examiners are the one nine that handled it roughest. The Suds men won a franchise-record 103 games, took the Central for the fourth consecutive year — no club had ever done it — and claimed the first seed of the whole field, closing at 18 won and 6 lost for September. Yet when they visited San Diego in August they were swept in three, their batsmen held to three hits in eight-and-twenty tries with runners in scoring position, and it was there that Jake Bauers, the thirty-year-old enjoying the season of his life, issued the prescription the clubhouse still quotes: "I just think we need to chill the [heck] out a little bit." They did — went straight to Dodger Stadium, took three of four, and never looked back. The Friars, for their own part, matched that 18-6 September stride for stride, needing every win of it to secure the league's top Wild Card berth, and arrive carrying a bullpen that has not yet surrendered a run this October, as this paper's Thursday columns recorded.

The pitching choices tell the whole strategy. San Diego passes over Buehler to start Robbie Ray, the left-hander got at the Deadline — for Milwaukee's order, first in the majors against right-handed pitching by the weighted measures, ranks but thirteenth against the southpaws, and Ray carries a career 2.82 figure against the Cream City club with a .193 average against. Milwaukee answers with the summit itself: Misiorowski, leader of all baseball in earned runs (1.80), strikeouts (252), base-runners per inning (0.80), and batting average allowed (.157). The hosts restored a bat for the occasion besides, activating Andrew Vaughn from the ten-day invalid rolls Friday. First pitch at half past eight; the first October meeting of the franchises born together in 1969 continues Sunday at four.

THE RESTING CHAMPIONS, A FULLER ACCOUNTING: OHTANI CONCEDES THE KNEE AND THE BICEPS MUST BE 'MANAGED' THROUGH OCTOBER — THE CHAMPIONS AWAIT THE RETURN OF A SWING LAST SEEN IN AUGUST

When this paper last took the champions' pulse, on the eve of the Wild Card round, Ohtani pronounced himself "feeling great physically"; Friday, speaking to the scribes for the first time since before his September stay on the invalid rolls, the four-time Most Valuable supplied the fuller ledger. The right biceps and the left knee that have troubled him since early summer remain unsolved. "I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this," said he through his interpreter. "That process is going to happen during the offseason... as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage." He will not pitch this postseason — the mound ambitions that produced 8 victories against 2 at a 1.79 figure through fourteen starts were shelved when the knee barked in July — and the bat's recent testimony is sobering: a .198 average with four-and-thirty strikeouts in the four-and-twenty games before his trip to the rolls, five hits in one-and-twenty tries upon his return, no home run since the eighteenth of August, and a season's total of thirty — his fewest in three Los Angeles summers — after six-and-twenty had come by midsummer at a .296 clip.

The bye week was spent on repairs: simulated at-bats against teammates and the pitching machine, rest for the joints, work for the timing. "I know that once the lights turn on, the postseason starts, the focus will be heightened," says the manager Roberts. "I expect good things. I really do. We just haven't seen it enough... for me to forecast it." The Herald, which entered the champion's own rosier bulletin in these columns Wednesday, enters Friday's candor beside it and lets the reader weigh the pair — observing only that a man who hits thirty home runs in a season his physicians would call lost remains a man no pitcher cares to see in October.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE MACHINE'S FIRST SEASON IS AUDITED — FOUR-AND-FIFTY OF EVERY HUNDRED CHALLENGED CALLS OVERTURNED, AND THE CATCHERS PROVE THE SHARPEST LAWYERS AT THE NEW BAR

The automated ball-strike system closed the books on its first regular season, and the audit makes agreeable reading for the challengers: four-and-fifty percent of all challenged calls were overturned, the human eye corrected by the machine more often than it was confirmed. The catchers proved far the most successful class of petitioner — fitting enough, for no man in the yard studies the strike zone at closer range — with the batsmen trailing well behind. This paper's readers have already seen the device's October debut: the first game-ending challenge in postseason history, raised by the catcher Realmuto in Philadelphia's Game Two resurrection, a called ball converted to strike three with the season in the balance — the new jurisprudence, as these columns recorded Thursday, arriving at the sport's biggest moments right on schedule.

And from the North Side, a first entry in the winter ledger this paper opened Thursday: the Cubs' operations chief Hoyer, surveying a lineup that scored one run in its two October games, declares the winter's first business will be the pitching — "pitching acquisition" the stated priority, with nothing, says he, off the table. The free agencies of Happ and Suzuki already stand on the docket; the North Side winter promises industry.

No tables this morning — Friday passed without a contest from coast to coast, the lone such pause the bracket will grant until the rounds are settled, and the Herald has spent it as the eight survivors did: in preparation. Today the quiet ends emphatically. Four Division Series open inside eight hours — Chicago at Cleveland at one o'clock, Atlanta at Los Angeles at four, New York at Tampa Bay at half past six, San Diego at Milwaukee at half past eight — and from this morning until the last pennant question is answered, every edition of this paper will carry October's fuller measure: no playoff game a two-sentence note, every contest given its full accounting. The morrow's number will bring the first four verdicts. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
