entry.title: THIRTY YEARS OF WINNER-TAKE-ALL SORROW, STRUCK FROM THE LEDGER IN NINE INNINGS — HARRIS GOLFS A SINKER THIRTEEN INCHES OFF THE EARTH FOR THREE, KERR THE ONCE-FORGOTTEN JOURNEYMAN BLANKS THE ORDER, AND SALE WALKS OUT OF THE BULLPEN TO BAR THE DOOR: ATLANTAS 6, PHILADELPHIAS 2, AND THE SERIES WITH IT
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 86 · Friday, the Second of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THIRTY YEARS OF WINNER-TAKE-ALL SORROW, STRUCK FROM THE LEDGER IN NINE INNINGS — HARRIS GOLFS A SINKER THIRTEEN INCHES OFF THE EARTH FOR THREE, KERR THE ONCE-FORGOTTEN JOURNEYMAN BLANKS THE ORDER, AND SALE WALKS OUT OF THE BULLPEN TO BAR THE DOOR: ATLANTAS 6, PHILADELPHIAS 2, AND THE SERIES WITH IT

Nola cannot find the plate and the hometown boy makes him pay the full tariff — a three-run thunderclap in the first on the lowest pitch ever hit for one of his hundred-and-one home runs — whereupon Albies and Olson add blasts of their own, three homers from the three men Philadelphia evicted from October in '22 and '23 alike; Kerr, told only Wednesday night he would open the decider, carves three and one-third one-hit innings out of the season's biggest game, and Sale, two days removed from ninety-five pitches, claims the final four outs to become the first man since his own 2018 self to start a series' first game and finish its last — Atlanta's first series won since the 2021 World Series, its first winner-take-all survived since the seventh game of the 1996 Championship Series, and a date with the twice-defending champion Dodgers on Saturday afternoon

Measure the decisive blow in inches, as the counting-men did. Aaron Nola's 2-0 sinker stood thirteen inches and a fraction above the Georgia clay — 1.11 feet, by the official instruments — when Michael Harris II reached down and golfed it on a line at a hundred miles the hour and a half more, Bryce Harper tracking it to the right-center wall only to watch it clear the brick by a hand's width. Three runs, first inning, and all the evening's scoring Atlanta would strictly require. The instruments pronounced it the lowest pitch ever converted into any of Harris's hundred-and-one home runs, the lowest Nola has ever had hit for one, and the third-lowest struck for a postseason homer since the tracking era began in 2008 — and it was hit by a son of the Atlanta soil, drafted by the home club out of its own suburbs, in the first winner-take-all October game of his life. Nola, who had walked Acuña and Olson on five pitches apiece to load the crisis and thrown but three of his first thirteen offerings for strikes, lasted five outs; Wheeler, the arm Philadelphia spent Sunday just to reach this round, gave four creditable innings of relief behind him, but the deficit had been dug.

The shutting of the door was a relay of improbables, and the first hand on it belonged to Ray Kerr. Told only Wednesday night that he would open the season's biggest game, the two-and-thirty-year-old left-hander — six weeks removed from Triple-A Gwinnett and the long road back from the 2024 elbow surgery — was handed the one assignment that mattered, the neutralizing of Schwarber and Harper atop the order, and he did that and more: three and one-third scoreless innings, a single hit, the Philadelphia bats carving at air. The man's history makes the arithmetic look small. A boyhood spent partly in foster homes while his father served time; a 2015 season pitching for a men's-league nine in Reno while clerking at a 7-Eleven and a movie house; and now the opener's ball in an October decider. "This was just another Thursday," said Kerr. "Growing up, I had a hard time. So, this was nothing." His manager Weiss put it otherwise: "Hopefully Ray Kerr became a bit of a household name tonight. He deserves it."

The middle chapters confirmed the verdict. Albies turned a Wheeler offering into the right-center seats with Riley aboard in the fourth, 5-0; Olson added a solo clout off Bowlan in the seventh — three home runs on the night, struck by the three Braves who were present to be evicted from October by these same Philadelphians in both 2022 and 2023, each man collecting a measure of his own account. The visitors' resistance came in polite installments: Schwarber came round on Bohm's sixth-inning groundout, and Derek Hill, having tripled in the eighth, scored on Turner's sacrifice fly — two runs, no more, against the procession of Holmes (two innings and the victory), Suarez, Fuentes, and Dodd.

And then the theater. Chris Sale — who had planted himself in Weiss's office chair in the afternoon before the manager could even raise the question, announcing "I feel amazing" — emerged from the bullpen in the eighth and struck out Harper to end it, then finished the ninth: four outs, a little more than eight-and-forty hours after throwing ninety-five pitches across six and one-third innings in Game One. The scribes certify him the first pitcher to start a series' opening game and close out that same series since one Chris Sale, Boston, World Series of 2018 — he and Kershaw now the only men to have done it twice. So fell a pair of droughts at a single stroke: Atlanta's first postseason series won since the 2021 World Series, and its first winner-take-all game survived since the seventh game of the 1996 Championship Series, six straight such defeats — the third-longest run of them in the annals — now closed. The application the Phils filed in these columns to become the fourth club of the best-of-three era to lose an opener and advance was denied without comment, before a sold-out Truist Park that stayed to watch the champagne. Next: the Division Series, Saturday at four o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, on the Fox circuits, with triple-digit heat in the forecast and the twice-defending champions waiting — a club Atlanta beat five times in six meetings this summer, outscoring them 26 to 15, for whatever such summer arithmetic is worth in October.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE EIGHT ARE NAMED AND THE CARD IS FULL — FOUR DIVISION SERIES OPEN SATURDAY FROM ONE O'CLOCK TO HALF PAST EIGHT, CLEVELAND HANDS ITS OPENER TO THE ROOKIE MESSICK, AND LOS ANGELES IS EXPECTED TO ANSWER ATLANTA WITH YAMAMOTO

The bracket's last blank is filled, and the schedule stands thus: Saturday the White Sox call at Cleveland at one o'clock, Atlanta at Los Angeles at four, the Yankees at Tampa Bay at half past six, and the Padres at Milwaukee at half past eight; the second games go Sunday at four in Milwaukee and eight in Los Angeles, Monday at five in Cleveland and eight in Tampa Bay, with Atlanta's series returning to Truist Park for a third game Tuesday evening. Friday carries not a contest anywhere in the land — the last quiet day before the four quarrels run concurrent.

Cleveland has shown its hand first. The manager Vogt names Parker Messick, the five-and-twenty-year-old rookie left-hander, for Game One against Chicago — a man who had to argue his way onto the roster in the spring and finished sixth in the game at a 2.56 figure, his three-and-ninety-and-a-hundred strikeouts the most by a Cleveland first-year man save Herb Score's 245 of 1955 — with Gavin Williams, whose 248 strikeouts led the American League and trailed only Misiorowski's 252 in all the game, to follow in Game Two. "They've been our two best pitchers," says Vogt. "They've earned it and then some." The Dodgers have made no formal announcement, but the expectation of the Los Angeles camp is Yamamoto for Game One — the only arrangement that returns their ace on regular rest for a fifth game, with Skubal, Snell, and Glasnow filling out a rotation of uncomfortable depth, and the Ohtani-Betts platoon atop the order sorting itself by the hand of the opposing starter. Atlanta, by contrast, arrives with its rotation depleted: Sale cannot go before Sunday's Game Two, Mahle not before Tuesday, and Pérez, on the invalid rolls since the first of September with the low back, not before Game Three — leaving Holmes, who threw but two innings Thursday, to be asked for the early innings Saturday, with young Ritchie an option and a left-handed opener under consideration besides.

THE PHILADELPHIA RECKONING: A FOURTH STRAIGHT OCTOBER SERIES SURRENDERED AND THE COSTLIEST CORE IN THE GAME AT A CROSSROADS — MATTINGLY DECLINES TO PLEAD HIS OWN CASE WHILE THE SHADOW OF CORA FALLS ACROSS THE INTERIM CHAIR

In the visitors' clubhouse Thursday night the beat men watched a group of Phillies — Schwarber, Realmuto, Turner, Stott, Nola, Stubbs — stand in a corner and talk quietly, and noted that it was not like the gatherings of a few years ago. The club has now surrendered four consecutive postseason series while carrying one of the heaviest payrolls in the game, and the Philadelphia correspondent pronounces changes not merely likely but overdue. "It's going to be a long offseason, obviously," said Harper. "I obviously have trust in the organization and people that are in charge. We'll see where we go."

The first question on the docket is the manager's chair. Mattingly, who took the club at 9-19 and steered it to the fourth-best record in the game thereafter — 79 won, 55 lost, and likely votes for Manager of the Year to come — declined to argue his own retention: "It's not the time to talk about anything like that. My stuff doesn't really matter." He reports no conversations with the front office on the subject. But the shadow over the interim chair has a name: the beat men record that Dombrowski offered the position to Alex Cora on the 26th of April, two days before Thomson's dismissal, that Cora declined it then, and that so long as Cora sits available and the interim tag stays unaddressed, the industry expects the pursuit to resume. The players, for their part, spoke for the incumbent — "his demeanor was great for us," testified Schwarber — while Harper, asked directly, declined the question. The Herald observes that a man who inherits a shipwreck in April and has it racing by June has earned at least a hearing in November.

THE DUGOUT DESK: ESPADA DECLARES HE WOULD 'ABSOLUTELY' RETURN TO A HOUSTON THAT HAS NOT YET SAID SO — WHILE ARIZONA, WANTING NO SUSPENSE, RETAINS LOVULLO ON NEW PAPER

The succession question this paper opened Thursday has its first testimony: Joe Espada, whose contract expired with Houston's elimination, declares he would "absolutely" like to return to the Astros in 2027. The club, which must also seat a new general manager, has not yet said whether the feeling is mutual — and the Herald notes that a manager auditioning for his own job while the office above him stands vacant is a delicate position even by Texas standards.

Arizona, meanwhile, declined to let any such question linger: the Diamondbacks retain Torey Lovullo on a new contract, the winningest manager in the franchise's annals across his ten seasons, now bound for an eleventh. One chair filled, one chair wobbling, and the music only beginning — the autumn's managerial carousel is hereby declared open.

THE ALMANAC DESK: FALL BALL IN THE DESERT — THE ARIZONA AUTUMN CIRCUIT OPENS ITS FOUR-AND-THIRTIETH SEASON SATURDAY, FIFTEEN OF THE GAME'S HUNDRED FINEST PROSPECTS ON THE ROLLS

While eight clubs quarrel over the pennants, the future reports for duty in the desert: the Arizona Fall League opens its four-and-thirtieth season Saturday, carrying fifteen members of the game's Top Hundred prospect list — matching the richest enrollment of the past four years. The rolls run from a seventeen-year-old, Angeibel Gomez, ranked one-and-eightieth in the game, to a nine-and-twenty-year-old in Tyler LaPorte, four winters a veteran of the independent circuits, with a genuine All-Star among them in the rehabilitating San Francisco closer Randy Rodriguez. The circuit's pedigree wants no argument — Judge, Trout, and Harper all took their autumn cuts there, former Fall League Most Valuables include Arenado, Acuña, and Bryant, and ten of the eighteen position men who started this summer's All-Star Game are alumni. Last autumn's Most Valuable, the Detroit infielder McGonigle, hit .362 in the desert and proceeded to lead the whole American League in wins above replacement at one-and-twenty this summer. The games count for nothing and foretell a great deal; the Herald will keep an eye on the box scores from the cactus country.

The Friday tables, then — one contest entered, and the Wild Card round closed at three days' length: four series, three settled by sweep, and the one that went the distance settled by the club that had waited thirty years to win a game of the winner-take-all kind. The field for the Division Series is therefore complete — Chicago's White Sox, Cleveland, New York, and Tampa Bay carrying the American's colors; Atlanta, Los Angeles, Milwaukee, and San Diego the National's — and today the land is quiet, not a game from coast to coast, the calm before four quarrels run at once. Saturday the cannonade: Chicago at Cleveland at one o'clock, Atlanta at Los Angeles at four, New York at Tampa Bay at half past six, San Diego at Milwaukee at half past eight. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO RUNS TO THE BAD AND SIX OUTS FROM WINTER, PHILADELPHIA ANSWERS WITH THREE THUNDERCLAPS — SCHWARBER AND HARPER BACK-TO-BACK IN THE EIGHTH, BOHM ALONE IN THE TENTH, AND THE MACHINE ITSELF CALLS THE FINAL STRIKE: PHILS 4, TOMAHAWK NINE 3, IN TEN INNINGS
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 85 · Thursday, the First of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 4 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO RUNS TO THE BAD AND SIX OUTS FROM WINTER, PHILADELPHIA ANSWERS WITH THREE THUNDERCLAPS — SCHWARBER AND HARPER BACK-TO-BACK IN THE EIGHTH, BOHM ALONE IN THE TENTH, AND THE MACHINE ITSELF CALLS THE FINAL STRIKE: PHILS 4, TOMAHAWK NINE 3, IN TEN INNINGS

Mahle gives Atlanta seven innings that deserved a kinder ledger and Harper's misplayed fly hands the hosts the lead besides — whereupon the Phils, measured for the coffin at 3-1, strike twice against Game One's winning pitcher and once against Fuentes in the tenth, young Painter takes his first taste of October and the victory with it, and Realmuto ends the night with the first game-ending ABS challenge in postseason history, sending the quarrel to a winner-take-all third chapter this very evening

Two runs to the bad and six outs from winter, Kyle Schwarber stood in against Dylan Lee — the man who had won Game One in relief — and swung Philadelphia's season back onto its hinges. One fly ball into the right-center seats; then Bryce Harper, the very next man, lifted another to nearly the same address; and a 3-1 deficit that had the undertakers out measuring was a 3-3 tie before Lee could record a second out. Two innings later Alec Bohm, two down in the tenth and nobody aboard, turned on Fuentes's offering and wrote the verdict into the right-field stands: 4-3, Phils, the series squared at a game apiece, and the club that stole the opener on Riley's eighth-inning thunder now made to play a third.

For seven innings it had belonged to Atlanta. Harper's first-inning single cashed Turner for 1-0, Olson's answered in the home half, and thereafter Tyler Mahle — 7-10 on the summer, as this paper's armory had him — gave seven innings of one-run, six-strikeout pitching that deserved a kinder ledger than the one he got. Sánchez, Philadelphia's eighteen-game winner, labored by comparison, five walks salted among his six and two-thirds, and the seventh inning cost him twice: Baldwin's catchable fly fell past Harper's misjudgment in right for a double, Murphy scoring, and Olson's sacrifice fly cashed Kim for 3-1 — the precise score from which the eighth-inning resurrection was conducted.

The last three innings belonged to a man playing his first October game. Andrew Painter, the young right-hander, took the ball with the season in his palm and gave three scoreless innings — three hits scattered, three strikeouts, not a run permitted — and claimed the victory for his trouble. The final pitch made history of its own denomination: Painter's two-out delivery to the pinch-hitter Smith, with two Braves aboard, was called a ball — whereupon the pitcher tapped his head, Realmuto tapped his in answer, and the automated arbiter reversed the call to strike three. The first game-ending challenge of a postseason, the league's scribes certify, and a ballgame concluded by nerve and machinery in equal parts.

So to this evening's decider — eight o'clock at Truist Park, on the NBC and Peacock circuits — and for once the probables ledger offers no names at all. "All hands on deck," declares the interim manager Mattingly of his pitching plans, while Atlanta weighs Holmes, who played coy on whether he starts or follows an opener, with Kerr and Suter among the arms behind him. The winner proceeds to the Division Series and the hundred-win Dodgers; and the Phils, should they prevail, would become but the fourth club of this best-of-three era to lose the opener and live to advance — by the very ledger this paper set out Wednesday.

The Postseason Card

ONE-AND-TWENTY YEARS BETWEEN OCTOBER HANDSHAKES — THE SOUTH SIDERS FINISH THE SAME HOUSTON CLUB THEY LAST BEAT IN THE 2005 WORLD SERIES, AND THE LONGEST WAIT IN THEIR LEDGER ENDS IN A SWEEP: SOUTH SIDERS 7, ASTROS 3

A four-run first inning batters the erstwhile invalid Brown before he can record a second out, Houston's three answers arrive politely one runner at a time, and Meidroth's three-run thunderclap in the sixth closes the account — whereupon Hicks and Fedde carry the hosts out hitless across the final four frames, fifteen Texans go down on strikes, and a club that lost one-and-twenty-and-a-hundred games two summers ago advances to meet Cleveland in the first October quarrel the Central neighbors have ever staged

The last time the White Sox won a postseason series, they were shaking hands on this same Houston club's infield — the World Series of 2005, swept in four. One-and-twenty years later they have done it again, in the same city, by the same emphatic method: a two-games-to-none sweep, sealed 7-3 Wednesday night beneath the closed roof at Daikin Park, and the South Siders — two summers removed from a season of one-and-twenty-and-a-hundred defeats, the worst in the modern annals — advance to a Division Series no spring prophecy dared sketch for them.

The verdict was effectively rendered in the first inning. Brown, the erstwhile invalid this paper's armory had opposite Burke, faced nine men and retired but two: Teel's single cashed Antonacci, Benintendi's line drive brought home Teel and Vargas both — the second run a gift of Spence's throwing error from center — and Peters's single made it 4-0 before Houston had drawn a clean breath. The hosts answered in polite installments, a solo blast apiece from Peña, Smith, and Altuve off Burke, who otherwise struck out eight in his four innings; and at 4-3 the issue stood until the sixth, when Chase Meidroth — whose series closes at four runs driven home — met a Lambert offering with two aboard, Luisangel Acuña and Peters scampering home ahead of him, 7-3. Thereafter the Chicago relay simply closed the yard: Kay for the win, then Hicks and Fedde two hitless innings apiece, fifteen Houston strikeouts entered in the final accounting, and not a run permitted across the last five frames.

The chairman Reinsdorf watched his improbable club celebrate on the road — the beat men report him savoring a run not a soul saw coming, the Vatican's correspondence excepted, as this paper recorded Wednesday. Now comes Cleveland: Game One of the Division Series goes Saturday at one o'clock on Lake Erie's shore, the first postseason meeting between these Central neighbors in the whole of their long acquaintance, and the form sheet is no comfort to the division champions — Chicago took seven of the thirteen between them this summer, six of the thirteen settled by a single run. Game Two follows Monday at five o'clock.

THE OLDEST QUARREL ENDS IN TWO SHORT CHAPTERS, AGAIN — FRIED CARVES SIX LEAN INNINGS, THE SIXTH POURS SIX MORE, AND BOSTON GOES HOME BY THE SAME OCTOBER DOOR AS LAST YEAR: PINSTRIPES 9, BOSTONS 2

García strikes the go-ahead blast in his first postseason start and Bellinger — on the night his father throws the ceremonial first pitch — drives home four, while the unsealed Crochet faces four men and retires none, Gray departs at seventy pitches wishing to 'live or die' with his manager's trust, and the Bombers advance on an aggregate of eighteen runs to two, bound for Tampa Bay and the top seed Saturday evening

For the second October running, the game's oldest quarrel was adjourned in the minimum two chapters, and by verdicts that brooked no appeal: 9-0 Tuesday, 9-2 Wednesday, eighteen runs to two across the series entire. Max Fried supplied the craftsmanship this time — six innings, three hits, a single run, six strikeouts — and the Yankee rotation, the beat men observe, now squares its shoulders with some confidence toward the rounds ahead.

The decisive blows were struck by the supporting cast. Luis García Jr., making his first postseason start, brought the Bronx to its feet with the game's first run — a fourth-inning blast, his first in October — and finished with three hits; Cody Bellinger, on the night his father Clay, once a Yankee himself, threw the ceremonial first pitch, drove home four, the last three aboard the home run that crowned a six-run sixth. That inning turned on Boston's most awaited arm: Crochet, the ace unsealed from the sixty-day rolls only on the series' eve — he may be needed at once, this paper wrote Wednesday, and so he was — faced four men without recording an out, three hits and four runs the toll. The visitors' griefs did not end there. Gray, the eighteen-game winner, was lifted at seventy pitches with but two runs against him, and did not disguise his feelings afterward — he wished his manager Tracy had let the game "live or die with me," said the right-hander, and the quarrel over the hook will season Boston's winter. The Hub nine's whole offense came to two solo blasts, Contreras's in the sixth — upheld by the review men — and Sogard's in the seventh; Chisholm, for good measure, stole two bases and scored twice for the hosts.

So New York proceeds, and the captain's calendar comes due: the Division Series date Judge's rehabilitation has had circled since the calf gave way now arrives Saturday at half past six in Tampa Bay, where the top-seeded Rays — the American's best by the season-long ledger — await a club they have met in October once before, the 2020 Division Series, settled in five for the Floridians. Game Two goes Monday at eight o'clock; whether the captain's name appears on the roster, the morrow's dispatches will tell.

FIVE ARMS BRAID A FIVE-HITTER AND THE WALKING BOOT COMES OFF SWINGING — SHEETS'S PINCH-HIT THUNDER SETTLES LAST OCTOBER'S ACCOUNT IN FULL: MISSION NINE 4, CUBS 1

Pivetta hands a lead to a bullpen that never gives it back, Salas at twenty becomes the youngest man ever to catch a postseason game and drives home a run for good measure, and when the Petco lights cut out for Miller's ninth the sweep is a formality — San Diego, ejected from this very round by these very Cubs a year ago, advances to Milwaukee and the hundred-three-win Cream City nine

San Diego closed out its revenge with the weapon it trusts most: the bullpen gate. Five Friar arms braided a five-hitter Wednesday night — Pivetta for three and a third, then Rodriguez for the win, Adam and Morejon holding, Miller sealing — and the Cubs, who ejected this club from the Wild Card round a year ago, were swept from it in two games flat, 4-1 the final, a single run their whole October's produce against eighteen innings of San Diego pitching.

The runs came in businesslike pairs. In the second, Bogaerts lined a single to cash France, and Ethan Salas — twenty years of age, and Wednesday the youngest man ever to catch a big-league postseason game — lifted a sacrifice fly for 2-0, a run driven home to garnish his history. Hoerner's single halved the lead in the fourth, Suzuki scoring; and in the home half Gavin Sheets, who passed most of September in a walking boot and entered now as a pinch-hitter, met the reliever Palencia's offering for a two-run blast, Bogaerts ahead of him, 4-1. Gausman, Chicago's starter, battled through three and a third and wore the loss. The ninth belonged to theater as much as to baseball: the Petco lights cut to black, the crowd rose roaring, and Mason Miller — the game's most feared closer, by the league's own estimate — struck out two around a harmless single to end the series, the sellout house never resuming its seats.

The form chart now sends the Friars north: Game One at Milwaukee Saturday at half past eight, Game Two Sunday at four o'clock, against the top-seeded, hundred-three-win Cream City nine — the first postseason meeting of two franchises born in the same expansion spring of 1969. The season's small ledger favors the visitors, four of six, including an August sweep at Petco Park; the Herald notes merely that the Friars arrive hot, rested by Friday's idle day, and carrying a bullpen that has yet to surrender a run this October.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THREE SWEEPS ENGRAVE THREE-QUARTERS OF THE DIVISION-SERIES CARD — CLEVELAND AND CHICAGO TO MEET IN OCTOBER FOR THE FIRST TIME IN THEIR LONG ACQUAINTANCE, NEW YORK RETURNS TO TAMPA BAY, AND MILWAUKEE AWAITS THE FRIARS

The bracket wants but one name. Three of the four Wild Card quarrels ended in two straight, and the league has published the consequences: the second-seeded Guardians entertain the sixth-seeded White Sox at Cleveland, Game One Saturday at one o'clock — the first postseason meeting between the Central neighbors in all their shared history, and a delicate matter for the hosts, who won the division yet dropped seven of thirteen to Chicago on the summer; Game Two goes Monday at five. The top-seeded Rays, the American's best by the full-season ledger, receive the Yankees Saturday at half past six, with Monday's Game Two at eight — those clubs having met once before in October, the 2020 Division Series, which Tampa Bay took in five. And the top-seeded Brewers host the Padres Saturday at half past eight, Game Two Sunday at four — the first postseason meeting of two franchises born together in 1969, the Friars having taken four of six between them this season.

The fourth line of the card is written tonight at Truist Park, its winner bound for the hundred-win Dodgers. Friday the second carries not a game anywhere in the land — a travel day for the fortunate, a first day of winter for the rest — and then Saturday the October proper begins.

THE BASEPATHS DESK: TWO BROTHERS, FOUR THEFTS, ONE AFTERNOON AND EVENING — RONALD AND LUISANGEL ACUÑA EACH STEAL TWICE IN A SINGLE INNING, AND THE WIRE PRONOUNCES IT POSTSEASON HISTORY

Wednesday's basepaths belonged to a single surname. In Atlanta, Ronald Acuña Jr. — held hitless by Philadelphia's pitching but twice issued passes — stole two bases in one inning against the Phils; in Houston, his younger brother Luisangel, running for Chicago as a pinch man, stole two in one inning against the Astros before coming round to score on Meidroth's home run. Two steals apiece, each pair inside a single frame, on the same day of the same October — a family feat the league's own wire pronounces postseason history, and this paper is pleased to enter in the annals. Pitchers of the surviving clubs are advised that one of the brothers remains at large in the bracket.

THE FRONT OFFICE DESK: HOUSTON'S OCTOBER LASTS TWO DAYS AND THE RECKONING BEGINS AT ONCE — A GENERAL MANAGER TO BE FOUND, AND THE MANAGER ESPADA'S STANDING THE OPEN QUESTION OF THE TEXAS WINTER

The Astros' season closed Wednesday night in their own yard, and the club walks into winter carrying an unusual vacancy: the general managership itself, which Houston must now fill even as it weighs the standing of the field manager Espada. The ledger the beat men recite is a sobering one for a once-imperial house — four years now since the World Series championship, three years since the club so much as won a postseason game, the great run of seven consecutive Championship Series appearances, four pennants, and two titles receding steadily into the rearview. The Herald observes that dynasties are dismantled on exactly such quiet Thursdays as this, one vacancy at a time, and will report the succession as it is decided.

THE WINTER LEDGER OPENS EARLY ON THE NORTH SIDE: THE CUBS DEPART OCTOBER WITH ONE RUN IN TWO GAMES AND A 'SOUR TASTE' FOR PROVISIONS — THE LOOMING FREE AGENCIES OF HAPP AND SUZUKI STAND FIRST ON THE WINTER'S DOCKET

For Chicago's National League tenants the abruptness is the wound: two October games, a single run scored between them, and a season of genuine promise closed before the calendar's first weekend. The beat men report the clubhouse tasting of what one of its number called the "sour taste" of the finish, and the front office already staring at the winter's first-order business — the looming free agencies of Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, two fixtures of the order now at the ends of their papers. The Herald notes that a lineup held to a single tally across eighteen October innings will spend four months hearing about it, and that the answers the North Side assembles by spring will say much about how long this particular window stays propped open.

The Thursday tables, then — four contests entered, and the Wild Card round all but spent: three series closed by sweep, the brooms wielded by the sixth seed in Houston, the fourth in the Bronx, and the fourth again in San Diego, while the lone survivor of the trailing clubs plays on. Tonight the round concludes where it began, Philadelphia at Atlanta at eight o'clock, winner to Los Angeles; Friday the schedule stands empty from coast to coast; and Saturday the Division Series open in three yards at once — Chicago at Cleveland at one, New York at Tampa Bay at half past six, San Diego at Milwaukee at half past eight. The Herald's Wednesday ledger bears repeating at the brink: in all the brief history of this best-of-three fashion, but three clubs have dropped the opener and lived to advance, and the Phils tonight apply to be the fourth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: SIX MONTHS OF FRUSTRATION, DISCHARGED IN ONE SWING — RILEY TURNS A NINE-AND-NINETY-MILE BULLET FROM PHILADELPHIA'S CLOSER INTO THREE EIGHTH-INNING RUNS, AND THE OLD OCTOBER ORDER IS OVERTURNED: BRAVES 5, QUAKERS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 84 · Wednesday, the Thirtieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 4 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX MONTHS OF FRUSTRATION, DISCHARGED IN ONE SWING — RILEY TURNS A NINE-AND-NINETY-MILE BULLET FROM PHILADELPHIA'S CLOSER INTO THREE EIGHTH-INNING RUNS, AND THE OLD OCTOBER ORDER IS OVERTURNED: BRAVES 5, QUAKERS 3

The opener at Truist Park is a seesaw of triples and nerve — Sale rises from his bed at dawn and strikes out nine, Luzardo makes a mockery of the word 'opener' with five sparkling innings, Realmuto's two-run three-bagger has Philadelphia ahead in the seventh — until Riley, with two out and two aboard in the eighth, meets Duran's 99.9-mile fastball and deposits it in the right-center seats, whereupon a club beaten by these same Quakers in three straight Octobers finds itself one victory from the Division Series

The first October afternoon at Truist Park was an argument that changed hands four times, and it ended on the fastest pitch Jhoan Duran could summon. Austin Riley — whose summer, by his own club's accounting, was six months of frustration in search of an afternoon like this one — came to the plate in the eighth with two out, two aboard, and Atlanta trailing 3-2. Duran reached back for 99.9 miles the hour. Riley met it flush and sent it to the right-center seats, and the yard shook, and the verdict was written: 5-3, Atlanta, and the first blood of the Wild Card round.

It was a proper duel long before it was a thunderclap. Chris Sale, making his first postseason start in five years, confessed he had been awake since first light — "I could have pitched this game at 8:15 this morning," said the ancient left-hander, and he pitched it at two o'clock like a man renewed: six and one-third innings, four hits, nine strikeouts, Harper fanned along the way with heat that touched three figures. Opposite him, Jesús Luzardo made comedy of the caution in his manager's vocabulary. Mattingly had called him an opener; the left-hander, whose whole September amounted to one four-pitch inning, gave five innings of three-hit, one-run pitching with six strikeouts, and handed the game over with Philadelphia ahead 1-0 on Bohm's first-inning double.

The middle chapters belonged to the three-baggers. Yastrzemski's single squared it in the second; Albies tripled home Harris in the sixth for 2-1; and in the seventh Realmuto answered with a two-run triple of his own — De La Cruz and Stott scampering home, 3-2 Philadelphia, and the visitors nine outs from the precise script of their last three October meetings with this club, every one of which the Quakers had won. Then came the eighth: Harris, three hits on the day, singled once more; Albies followed him aboard; and Riley closed the ledger. Lee took the win in relief, Iglesias closed the ninth, and Duran — an All-Star all summer — wore the loss and the blown save together.

The arithmetic of the best-of-three is now brutally simple. Atlanta, which took nine of thirteen from Philadelphia this season and had never beaten them in October, leads one game to none and can end the affair this very afternoon: Game Two goes at two o'clock at Truist Park, Sánchez (18-7, a 2.91 figure) — fully rested, as this paper noted in yesterday's armory — against Mahle (7-10, 3.99). The survivor of the series calls upon the hundred-win Dodgers when the Division Series opens Saturday, the third of October; the Quakers, for their part, must now win twice in two days or watch a fifth consecutive October end at its first station.

The Postseason Card

THE STUMBLE AT THE DUGOUT STEP IS THE ONLY ONE ALL EVENING — ANTONACCI TRIPS AT THE INTRODUCTIONS, THEN TREADS ON HOUSTON FOR NINE INNINGS: WHITE STOCKINGS 6, HOUSTONS 3

The 84-win guests arrive at the 81-win champions' yard and play the part of the better club from the first frame — three runs before the second inning is done, Colson Montgomery's thunderclap in the fourth, and a bullpen relay that ends with young Taylor emptying the tank across a career-long two and one-third — while in the eighth the hosts' last uprising dies at the feet of Yainer Diaz, and word arrives that the Vatican itself had written the South Side ahead of the series

The evening's augury came at the pregame introductions, when Sam Antonacci tripped running out of the dugout at Daikin Park — and it proved a false omen entirely, for that misstep was very nearly Chicago's last. The White Stockings, whose 84 victories exceed their hosts' 81 — the curiosity this paper has twice remarked now made flesh — struck the champions of the West early and never surrendered the lead: Murakami's sacrifice fly cashed Antonacci in the first, and in the second Antonacci himself lined a single that brought home Braden Montgomery and Meidroth both, 3-0, before Houston's relay of arms had found its footing. The opener Blubaugh, undone by three walks in two-thirds of an inning, wore the loss; his successor King was raked for four hits in a third.

Colson Montgomery's solo thunderbolt in the fourth made it 4-0, Meidroth singled home a fifth in the fifth, and when Velázquez answered with a two-run blast for Houston, Murakami came home on a wild pitch to restore the four-run distance. The arithmetic thereafter belonged to Chicago's bullpen — Smith opening with three spotless innings, Hicks taking the win — and above all to Grant Taylor, summoned with two out in the seventh, who in the eighth met the evening's one true crisis — runners at first and second, two out, a three-run lead, and the dangerous Diaz at the plate — and put out the fire and finished the game besides: two and one-third innings, five strikeouts, the longest outing of his young life. Houston's final tally required an error to score. And for benediction, the club revealed that Pope Leo XIV — a White Sox man of long standing, who sat in the Rate Field seats for the 2005 World Series against these very Astros — had sent a letter to the chairman Reinsdorf ahead of the series, commending the club's fostering of friendship and solidarity through sport. The South Side, it appears, holds accounts in every ledger.

So a club that had not played an October game since 2021 leads its series one game to none, and the champions of the West — who took five of seven from Chicago this summer, and whose season was saved from a 20-31 May by main strength — stand in a must-win posture at their own yard. Game Two goes at five o'clock this evening at Daikin Park: Burke (11-7, 3.34) for the visitors against Brown (6-4, 3.19), the erstwhile invalid, for the hosts. The survivor of the series travels to Cleveland, where the Division Series opens Saturday, the third of October.

TWO SONS OF MASSACHUSETTS BREAK NEW ENGLAND'S HEART IN THE BRONX — SCHLITTLER STRIKES OUT TEN, RICE STRIKES A GRAND SLAM, AND THE OLDEST QUARREL OPENS AT NINE TO NOTHING: BRONX BOMBERS 9, CRIMSON HOSE 0

The seventh October chapter of the game's oldest feud begins as a taut 2-0 affair and ends an avalanche — Schlittler, who closed Boston's season a year ago, gives six and one-third two-hit innings; Rice, faithful to his scrambled eggs and avocado toast, collects four hits, two home runs, and six runs driven in; young Lombard makes a three-hit postseason debut; and Boston's miseries multiply when Anthony departs the sixth with the old right hand barking anew

New York's Game One plan was executed by two men raised in the shadow of the enemy's cathedral. Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, Massachusetts boys the both, grew up surrounded by everything Red Sox — and in the seventh postseason meeting of the game's oldest quarrel they dismantled the club of their boyhood with a thoroughness that will be remembered on both sides of the line. Schlittler, owner of the American's best earned-run figure at 1.95 and the man who ended Boston's season in last October's Game Three, gave six and one-third innings of two-hit, scoreless pitching with ten strikeouts; Rice, a man of iron routine — the same cage work daily, the same breakfast of scrambled eggs and avocado toast — went four for five with a double, a fifth-inning home run, and, for punctuation, an eighth-inning grand slam: six runs driven in on the night.

For six innings it was nonetheless a duel worthy of the rivalry. Payton Tolle — at three-and-twenty the third-youngest man ever to start a Boston postseason opener, as this paper recorded yesterday, behind only Wood of 1912 and Ruth of 1918 — acquitted himself with honor: four and two-thirds innings, one run, the game still within a swing's reach at 2-0 when he departed. Then the Boston bullpen came apart at the seams — two in the seventh, five in the eighth, the last four aboard Rice's slam — while Wells drove home two and George Lombard Jr., the boy wonder whose first big-league hit, this very summer, was a home run, rapped three hits in his first taste of October. "Locked in," his teammates called him; the box score concurs.

Boston's deeper wound may be the one in the sixth inning's margin: Roman Anthony, checked swings having set the old right hand to barking, left the game and was hit for by Monasterio — the same hand whose partially torn ring-finger tendon cost him a stretch of the summer. "Hard to say right now," said the manager Tracy of his availability for Game Two, and the club must weigh the crueler arithmetic of an injury replacement, which would bar him until the Championship Series. There was one entry on the credit side of Boston's ward ledger: the ace Crochet, unseen since April, was formally activated from the sixty-day rolls on the eve of the series, the crate at last unsealed. He may be needed at once — Game Two goes at eight o'clock this evening in the Bronx, the wins leader Gray (18-5, 2.72) against Fried (5-5, 2.80), with the survivor of the series bound for Tampa Bay and Saturday's Division Series, and Boston bound for winter if it cannot solve the Bombers twice running.

SEVEN INNINGS WITHOUT A HIT UNTIL A DRIBBLER SPOILS THE SCROLL — KING FLIRTS WITH OCTOBER IMMORTALITY, THREE THUNDERCLAPS DO THE REST, AND MUSGROVE WALKS OUT OF TWO LOST YEARS INTO A ROARING PETCO NIGHT: GASLAMP NINE 8, CUBS 0

Last October's tormentors are made to pay for it with interest — Tatis and Machado strike home runs before the first inning is out, Bogaerts adds a third, and King carries a no-hitter to one out in the seventh, the longest such October errand since 2019, before Hoerner's forty-foot roller writes the only line in Chicago's hit column against him; then, with the verdict long settled, the hometown right-hander Musgrove takes a big-league mound for the first time since 2024 and the Gaslamp Quarter forgets the score entirely

San Diego opened its October by settling last year's account with compound interest. The Cubs, who ejected the Friars from the Wild Card round a year ago and had taken five of six from them in the season just closed, were handed the most comprehensive defeat of the young postseason: 8-0, thirteen hits against three, and for seven innings the genuine prospect of an ignominy without precedent in their October annals. Michael King, handed a 2-0 lead before the first inning was done, carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning — the longest postseason no-hit bid since Aníbal Sánchez's seven and two-thirds in the 2019 Championship Series — until, with one out, Hoerner topped a forty-foot dribbler down the third-base line that no arm in the yard could have converted. "When you're going out in the seventh with a no-hitter — you definitely are thinking about it," King allowed afterward. His final line wanted nothing for the loss of the scroll: seven innings, the one hit, eight strikeouts, and heat that touched 97.6 — his liveliest in three years.

The thunder had come early and kept its own counsel. Tatis opened the home first with a home run and Machado followed him two batters later with another — 2-0 before the Gaslamp crowd had settled — and the pair kept at it: Machado's double cashed Tatis in the third, Bogaerts struck the third homer in the fourth, and a five-spot's worth of industry in the middle innings (Merrill's two-run single and a passed ball among the freight) ran it to seven. Boyd, Chicago's Game One starter, was charged with three home runs inside four innings and the loss. The Cubs' three hits were their fewest consolation; their ace question now presses, for the sore-shouldered Gausman — whose non-throwing shoulder this paper reported under the trainers' watch — takes the ball tonight after all.

The ninth inning belonged to sentiment. Joe Musgrove, the San Diegan who had not stood on a big-league mound since 2024 — activated from the sixty-day rolls only this week after the long road back — walked out of two lost years and into a roaring Petco night, and worked a scoreless ninth around two hits and a walk, striking out a pair, while the score ceased to matter to anyone in the yard. The series stands one game to none for the Gaslamp nine; Game Two goes at ten o'clock this evening at Petco Park, Gausman (9-12, 4.51) against Pivetta (3-2, 2.86), whose own summer was five months lost to a flexor strain. The survivor travels to Milwaukee and its hundred-three-win hosts for Saturday's Division Series; the Cubs must now take two straight from a club they could not touch for seven innings.

News Around the League

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE, DECIDED: JUDGE IS LEFT OFF THE WILD CARD ROLLS — ALL HIS CONVINCING COULD NOT OUTRUN A CALF THAT WANTS THREE WEEKS, THOUGH STANTON AND GRISHAM RETURN TO THE COLORS

The verdict this paper promised its readers arrived before the Bronx first pitch, and it went against the plaintiff: Aaron Judge was not added to New York's Wild Card roster. The captain had spent the idle Monday pleading his case in live batting practice — "I've been doing a lot of convincing," he said — but the medical men were not converted. "I don't think he's all the way back," ruled the manager Boone, while calling the progress encouraging; the moderate strain of the right calf's soleus muscle, treated by injection a week ago, ordinarily asks three weeks that the calendar refused to give. The captain's hopes now ride on his teammates: should they pass Boston, the Division Series opens Saturday, and his rehabilitation continues with that date circled — he intends, he has said, to return a full right fielder, not a borrowed bat.

The same roster that closed its door on the captain opened it to two other invalids: Giancarlo Stanton was activated from the sixty-day rolls, and Trent Grisham from the ten-day, the latter patrolling center field before the Game One evening was out. The Herald observes that a 9-0 verdict, entered elsewhere in this number, was obtained without any of the three.

THE HERALD DIPS ITS CAP: HENDRIKS, THE AUSTRALIAN WHO BEAT CANCER BETWEEN SAVES, CALLS IT A CAREER — 'MY ARM HAS TOLD ME IN NO UNCERTAIN TERMS THAT IT HAS EXACTLY ZERO FASTBALLS LEFT IN IT'

Liam Hendriks, seven-and-thirty years of age and fourteen seasons a big-leaguer, announced his retirement Tuesday, and the game is poorer for the quiet. The Australian right-hander leaves a ledger of 490 games and some six hundred sixty-three innings at a 3.88 figure — a 3.16 in relief, where his fame was made: Reliever of the Year in the American League in both 2020 and 2021, thrice an All-Star, and the only man from his continent ever selected more than once. The sternest save of his life was recorded off the field: diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in January of 2023, he took three months of chemotherapy and stood cancer-free by May, Comeback Player of the Year before the season was out, and seven times a nominee for the Clemente award besides. His farewell was in character — no ceremony, only candor: "My arm has told me in no uncertain terms that it has exactly zero fastballs left in it." The Herald submits that the arm gave fair value, and dips its cap to a workingman of the bullpen who never once shorted the till.

THE PURSE DESK: THE NEW MAN POHLAD VOWS THE TWINS WILL 'MEANINGFULLY INVEST' AND CONTEND IN 2027 — THE HERALD ENTERS THE PLEDGE IN PENCIL, THE PAYROLL LEDGER BEING WRITTEN IN INK

In Minnesota, where the faithful have watched an Opening Day payroll of some $153.7 million in 2023 whittled to roughly $109.5 million — two-and-twentieth among the thirty clubs — the franchise's newly designated control man, Tom Pohlad, met the press and made promises. "I understand the patience in this market has run out, and I assure you we have a sense of urgency," said he, vowing the ownership will "meaningfully invest" in the payroll and contend in 2027, though declining to attach a figure to the meaning. The Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of record, notes that the pledge follows a 77-85 season, a 2025 deadline selloff of uncommon aggression, and three years of the ledger running steadily the other way — and that the ballplayer, unlike the promise, must be paid in currency. The pledge is entered in pencil accordingly; the winter's signings will show whether it deserves ink.

THE RESTING CHAMPIONS: OHTANI PRONOUNCES HIMSELF 'FEELING GREAT' AND WILL SWING STRAIGHT THROUGH THE BYE — FREEMAN SPENDS THE IDLE WEEK IN SEARCH OF THE SWING SEPTEMBER TOOK FROM HIM

From the camp of the hundred-win Dodgers, idle until Saturday's Division Series against the survivor of the Atlanta-Philadelphia quarrel, two bulletins on the state of the machinery. Shohei Ohtani reports himself "feeling great physically" and will continue to hit through the bye week rather than rest the bat — the club expecting him restored to full menace atop the order when the games resume. Freddie Freeman, meanwhile, puts the idle days to humbler use: the eight-time All-Star, whose September was a rough one by his own accounting, is at work rediscovering the swing, professing as ever the power of mind over matter. The Herald notes that clubs which earn the bye are entitled to spend it as they please, and that there are worse omens for the rest of the field than the champions treating a week of rest as a week of work.

The Wednesday tables, then — four contests entered at October's fuller measure, as this paper promised when it retired the summer economy, and the opening night's ledger reads: three hosts held serve, and one guest, the 84-win White Stockings, stole a march in Texas. Tonight the four quarrels resume at the same hours — Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock, the White Stockings at Houston at five, Boston in the Bronx at eight, the Cubs at San Diego at ten — and every one of the four leaders can close its series where it stands, while every trailer plays for the right to see Thursday, when the deciding games would go in the same yards. The trailing clubs may take what comfort history offers, which is little: in four-and-twenty prior series of this best-of-three fashion, but three clubs have lost the opener and lived to advance, and two of those in the spectatorless autumn of 2020. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Nine-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 83 · Tuesday, the Nine-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the Wild Card Series Openers (Tuesday, the Nine-and-Twentieth of September).

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE IDLE DAY IS SPENT AND THE WAITING ENDS AT TWO O'CLOCK — FOUR GAME ONES BETWEEN THE MATINEE HOUR AND THE STROKE OF MIDNIGHT, AND EVERY ARM THAT WILL THROW THE FIRST PITCH NOW KNOWN BY NAME

Monday passed exactly as this paper foretold in its last dispatch: not a ball was pitched in anger anywhere in the land, the twelve traveled and talked and took their batting practice behind closed gates, and the only scores kept were at the press conferences. The vigil ends this very day. Four best-of-three series open this afternoon and evening, every game at the higher seed's park, carried on the NBC and Peacock circuits with ESPN Radio crying the action coast to coast.

The card, in order of first pitch, with the duelists now confirmed by the league's own probable-pitcher ledger: Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock at Truist Park, Luzardo (14-5, a 2.86 figure, two hundred one-and-twenty strikeouts) against the grizzled southpaw Sale (14-9, 2.16); the White Sox at Houston at five o'clock at Daikin Park, the rookie Smith (3-3, but a 1.29 figure) against the rookie Blubaugh (5-3, 3.66); Boston at New York at eight o'clock in the Bronx, the rookie Tolle (9-6, 3.03) against Schlittler and his league-best 1.95; and the Cubs at San Diego at ten o'clock at Petco Park, Boyd (10-5, 3.91) against King (12-10, 3.21).

The wage of survival is engraved already: the winners advance to the Division Series opening Saturday, the third of October — Boston's or New York's survivor to Tampa Bay, the Houston series' survivor to Cleveland, the survivor of the San Diego series to Milwaukee, and Philadelphia's or Atlanta's to the hundred-win Dodgers, each at the resting club's yard. Of the four openers the armory desk below gives the particulars, for every one of them carries a story.

THE ARMORY DESK: BOSTON HANDS ITS OPENER TO A MAN YOUNGER THAN ANY SINCE RUTH — COUNSELL SHOWS HIS HAND AT LAST, MATTINGLY SAYS 'START' BUT MEANS 'OPEN,' AND HOUSTON'S DUEL IS A BULLPEN DAY ON BOTH SIDES

The deliberations this paper has chronicled all resolved themselves on the idle Monday, and each resolution repays study. In New York, the manager Tracy passed over his eighteen-game winner Gray and handed Game One to Payton Tolle, three-and-twenty years and three hundred two-and-thirty days of age — the third-youngest man ever to start the first game of a Boston postseason, behind only Smoky Joe Wood of the 1912 World Series and one George Herman Ruth of the 1918. The logic wants no defending: in two starts against these same Yankees the rookie went unbeaten with a 0.69 figure, eighteen strikeouts, and a .093 average against. Opposite him stands Schlittler, who ended Boston's season in last October's Game Three and greets the rematch with relish; Gray takes Game Two.

In Chicago's camp, the hand so long held against the chest — as this paper noted only yesterday — was laid on the table at the eleventh hour: Boyd starts the opener at Petco Park, with Imanaga, Holmes, Peterson, and the sore-shouldered Gausman held in reserve behind him, that last name under the trainers' watch for soreness in the non-throwing shoulder. San Diego answers with its ace King, then likely Pivetta, whose summer was five months lost to a flexor strain. In Philadelphia's camp the word 'start' required amendment: "I should say open," said the interim manager Mattingly of Luzardo, whose whole September amounts to Sunday's four-pitch eighth inning, and whose leash will be short accordingly; Sánchez, fully rested, takes Wednesday's Game Two. And at Daikin Park the afternoon is a bullpen day on both sides of the ledger: Venable's Smith — eight-and-twenty innings of big-league life, and ugly swings induced all the while — opens what his manager plainly calls a bullpen-type game, while Houston counters with Blubaugh as the opener of its own relay, the young man having thrown but fifteen pitches since Friday.

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE: JUDGE PLEADS BEFORE THE ROSTER COURT WITH A CALF THAT WANTS THREE WEEKS AND A CALENDAR THAT GIVES HIM HOURS — 'I'VE BEEN DOING A LOT OF CONVINCING,' SAYS THE MAN, AND THE CONVINCING CONTINUES

The question this paper left open on Monday — whether the Yankee captain's September calf permits him an October — came no nearer its answer on the idle day, though not for want of advocacy. The injury is a moderate strain of the soleus muscle of the right calf, a hurt that ordinarily asks three weeks' healing; the calendar offers considerably less. Judge spent Monday making his case in every available court: four turns at the plate in live batting practice — two walks drawn, a called third strike, a ground ball to the mound — with his running still confined to the anti-gravity treadmill, no stride yet taken on open grass, let alone a cut on the basepaths.

"I've been doing a lot of convincing," said the reigning Most Valuable, "and I'm going to keep doing that." The manager Boone holds the judicial tone — the club prepares as though its captain will not serve, while declining to rule him out; if the medical men give their blessing, the roster has his name on it within the hour. "He's making progress," is as far as Boone will be drawn. The candor of the plaintiff himself deserves entry in the record: "Guys take risks every single day. I understand the risks. I've got it all." The roster is due before this evening's first pitch, and the Herald will report the verdict on the morrow.

THE SPEEDSTER'S DESK: A MAN WHO HAS NEVER PLAYED A BIG-LEAGUE INNING MAY DEBUT IN THE POSTSEASON ITSELF — BOSTON WEIGHS BRAIDEN WARD, HIRED FOR HIS LEGS ALONE, WITH AN OLD 2004 GHOST SMILING ON THE ENTERPRISE

Among the papers Boston must file before tonight's opener is one that would make history of a rare denomination: should the club carry Braiden Ward, the seven-and-twenty-year-old outfielder would become but the seventh man in the game's annals to make his Major League debut in the postseason, and the first of Boston's ever to do so. The résumé is a single sentence long and needs no second: six minor-league seasons, two hundred two-and-seventy stolen bases in five hundred three-and-twenty games, and this summer at Worcester a franchise-record one-and-sixty thefts against nine times caught. He would be carried to do one thing only, and every soul in the park would know the thing, and he would attempt it anyway.

"It's like a dream. It's like a fever dream," said the stringbean — five feet nine, a hundred sixty pounds, and by the beat men's account he talks as fast as he runs. "One day I'm in Worcester, the next day I'm at the nicest hotel I've ever stayed at in New York City with the greatest team, getting to hopefully play in the greatest rivalry." The precedent wants no explaining in that rivalry's precincts: a borrowed pair of legs, a ninth inning in the Bronx, October of 2004 — Roberts stole, Mueller singled, and Boston never lost again. The Herald offers no prophecy, only the observation that history has a weakness for fast men in October.

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: SEATTLE OPENS ITS SEARCH WANTING GRAY HAIRS AND FRESH THOUGHT AT ONCE — AND THE FIRST NAME ON ITS SLATE, THE RUMOR WIRE REPORTS, IS THE VERY MAN WHO ASKED ONLY TO BE WANTED

The vacancy this paper recorded on Monday morning acquired its first candidates by Monday evening. Dipoto, Seattle's baseball chief these eleven years, met the press on the managerial question and set out his specification: unlike Wilson and Servais before him, the next man will have managed in the big leagues — "We need fresh thought," said he, calling for a reset of the culture entire, and adding, with a confidence the 76-86 ledger does not entirely underwrite, that not a candidate in baseball would fail to be excited by the post.

And the first name on the slate, the rumor wire reports through the Seattle Times' account, is one this paper's readers met only yesterday in a San Diego clubhouse doorway: Torey Lovullo, ten years in the Arizona chair, 750-768 with a pennant among the honors, his contract expired and his wish — "I just want to be wanted" — now perhaps to be granted on Puget Sound. Industry men count him among the leading candidates. The remainder of the reported slate runs to Vogt of Cleveland — twice running the American's Manager of the Year, winterer in Olympia, and all but unobtainable, being under contract to a champion; prying him loose would want a trade of the kind not seen since Piniella went to Tampa for an outfielder in 2002 — with Baldelli, Woodward, and Hyde the further names entered. The Herald observes that a man dismissed for finishing 86-76 may yet be hired by a club that finished ten games worse, and that there is a sermon in that somewhere.

THE WAIVER WIRE: ONE SMALL ENTRY ON AN OTHERWISE EMPTY LEDGER — ST. LOUIS CLAIMS THE RIGHT-HANDER HAMPTON FROM WASHINGTON

The transaction column, on a day the whole game held its breath, carried a single line: the Cardinals claimed the right-handed pitcher Chase Hampton off waivers from the Nationals — a winter lottery ticket punched while every other front office in the land was printing October rosters. The Mound City club, its season done these two days, thus fires the offseason's first quiet shot; the Herald enters it in the ledger and moves along to weightier matters.

The Tuesday tables, then — no contests to enter, the pennant races resting one last breath, and the vigil of the idle day kept faithfully to its end. It ends tonight: Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock, the White Sox at Houston at five, Boston in the Bronx at eight, the Cubs at San Diego at ten, four Game Ones stretched from matinee to midnight, and by the small hours the first four verdicts of October will be in. The morrow's dispatch will enter every one of them at October's fuller measure — the summer economy is hereby retired for the season, and each game shall have its full column. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
